The Good:

- The simulated computer UI is slick and responsive, and very immersive (so long if you suspend disbelief that technology was this advanced in the early 90s lol).
- The soundtrack perfectly sets the mood.
- Most of the connections between clues are interesting and fun to figure out.
- The story is engaging and well-paced.

The Bad:

- The game is too short! Most of my other points are variations of this complaint.
- Not enough cases/clues, so the central mystery builds extremely quickly.
- Some tools you use only once.
- The ending is rather abrupt and either downbeat or an annoying cliffhanger, depending on your perspective.
- Player choice is largely an illusion. Depending on choices, some events play out slightly differently and a tiny bit more of the backstory is revealed or not, but 95% of the story is identical, including the ending.
- Voice acting is fine, but not amazing
- All this feels like a hook for a (hopefully larger and longer) sequel

All in all though, the quality of what IS in the game plus its low price moves it to the recommend column for me. It is up to you if a game you can beat in a sitting or two is worth whatever price it is at the moment. For me, it was.

[h1]Game Review: The Operator[/h1]

[b]Playtime:[/b] 4h
[b]Status:[/b] Completed

The Operator is incredibly fun for its short four-hour runtime.

It is perfect for people who enjoy puzzles and want to feel intelligent while connecting clues. The gameplay is simple, satisfying, and immediately hooks you. The story builds tension well, and the music supports the atmosphere perfectly.

For most of the game, it feels like you have many possible paths.

Unfortunately, that is mostly an illusion.

[spoiler]The story is completely linear, there is only one ending, and it arrives abruptly without a satisfying payoff.[/spoiler]

That leaves a bad aftertaste, even though the four hours before it were great.

[b]7/10 — excellent short-term fun, disappointing ending.[/b]

I have depression. Playing games is one of a few ways I try to take my mind off of things that would typically worsen that depression, something that is proving exceptionally more difficult at the time of this writing. I actively avoid media that would obviously worsen that depression. I keep up on my anti-depression meds. This is how I take care of myself.

People are free to enjoy the media that they enjoy, and some people will, and have, really enjoyed this game. I won't fault people for that. As much as I hate to say it, I think I'm probably a case study for why some things need content warnings, because I'm going to be carrying this game's ending with me now and I really wish I didn't have to carry that on top of everything else I deal with on a day-to-day basis.

That said, I will not be directly spoiling anything. I went in blind, which if you're like me, I strongly advise you not to do. Watch a playthrough, or preferably just read up on the community posts first. Those'll mostly tell you all you need to know whether this is a game you'll be able to enjoy or not.

All that aside, the investigative gameplay was great, but a little lacking. They introduce tools and mechanics you use once and never again, which feels like a lot of wasted potential.

Again, if you're like me and prefer to play games to escape having to dwell on all the problems with real life, I advise you to give this game a pass and instead, pick up Scrutinized and play it on Detective Mode. Similar gameplay without reminding you quite as much about how much you really hate some aspects of the world you live in.

I think if I weren't in the mental state I'm in, I probably would have enjoyed the game more, and even appreciated the ending more. It is certainly realistic. It wraps up exactly how I would expect this scenario to end in the real world. I think that's why I hate it. It's just reaffirmation that good things don't actually happen to good people. Something I was already well aware of, and really didn't need a reminder.

There was a lot of effort put into this game, but I'm not quite sure if it paid off for me. The main storyline was predictable, no red herrings or distractions from this main plot. There are no consequences to any of the choices I made. Like no matter what option I picked, I was going to get the same outcome - I'd rather fail and have a rewind to try an interaction again. 

I really enjoyed some of the mechanisms that were set up - identifying cars, substances, and etc. I wish there was more of them, and a bit more substance to it rather than just clicking and having pop-ups. An example of having more substance would be if I had a car identifying task I get given a line up of cars to choose from to deduce the correct one. Or if there was a gunshot I'd have to analyse it at least a little bit, like the angle of how the shot happened could help deduce the height of the killer. But no, after I scrape the surface of a puzzle I'm pushed back into the strict dialogue. 

Some of the visuals were really silly and took me out of the immersions, [spoiler]like why was Kathrine 3ft in the hallway, and 5ft10 in the locker room[/spoiler], especially when juxtaposed to real headshots of real humans, as well as illustrations. 

As of writing this, I've completed the main storyline in 3 hours. Wasn't worth it for me.

The Operator — Quick Review

Platform: PC (Steam)

Genre: Puzzle / Simulation / Mystery

Verdict: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ A standout puzzle experience

---

What It Is

The Operator puts you in the role of a remote operator—essentially a digital detective working through cases from behind a screen. You dig through databases, analyze evidence, make phone calls, and piece together mysteries using a realistic desktop interface. It's the kind of game that makes you feel like you're actually doing the job.

Why It Works

The puzzle design is the star. The game doesn't hold your hand. You're given tools, a case file, and just enough rope to figure things out yourself. The satisfaction of connecting two pieces of evidence you found hours apart is genuinely rewarding. It respects your intelligence in a way few puzzle games do.

The interface feels authentic. The fake desktop OS, the clunky database searches, the phone calls—it all adds to the immersion. You're not just solving puzzles; you're inhabiting a role.

The layered structure keeps it fresh. Each case builds on what you've learned, but introduces new mechanics or twists so it never feels repetitive. By the time you've played "a couple layers" (as you put it), the game has opened up into something much deeper than it first appears.

The Vibe

It's methodical. Deliberate. If you want fast-paced action, this isn't it. But if you enjoy the slow burn of untangling a mystery—cross-referencing names, verifying alibis, catching contradictions—The Operator is incredibly satisfying.

Bottom Line

One of the better puzzle experiences on Steam right now. It trusts the player, delivers great "aha!" moments, and wraps it in a polished, believable package. Highly recommended if you enjoy games like Papers, Please, Orwell, or Return of the Obra Dinn.

[h2]The Operator[/h2]

There's a specific kind of satisfaction in being handed a suite of official-looking software and told to go find the truth. The Operator gets that feeling exactly right. You sit at your FDI terminal running facial recognition, pulling phone records, cross-referencing databases, and matching evidence, and the tools are just fiddly and authentic enough that every solved case feels like [i]you[/i] cracked it rather than the game waving you through. Nothing lands harder than dragging two pieces of evidence together on a hunch and watching the system confirm you were right.

What surprised me is how well the story holds it all up. The FMV performances could have been cheesy but they're played straight enough to sell a conspiracy that keeps widening in ways I didn't see coming, and the whole thing is wrapped in a moody, convincingly bureaucratic atmosphere that makes a desk job feel tense. It's not a long game, but it's a tight one, and it never overstays its welcome. [b]Recommended[/b], especially if you like detective work that actually makes you think instead of just clicking the obvious next thing.

The Operator is a narrative-driven game where you step into the role of an FDI Agent, solving criminal cases by analyzing evidence, searching databases, and assisting field agents.

The game gives you the illusion of meaningful choices, but in reality it's a fairly linear experience. No matter what decisions you make, the story ultimately follows the same path. If you're expecting multiple endings or a branching narrative where your choices have lasting consequences, you may end up disappointed.

That said, if you're looking for an engaging, story-focused experience to relax with on a lazy Sunday afternoon, The Operator absolutely delivers. The investigations are entertaining, the atmosphere is great, and the gameplay does a good job of making you feel like you're working behind the scenes as an investigator. As long as you go in expecting an interactive story rather than a true choice-driven adventure, you'll likely have a great time.

The Operator is somewhat summed up as an detective esk simulator game where the bulk of the gamelay loop is behind your desk, gathering evidence & solving cases by connecting the dots. It was clearly inspired by games such as Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You, Song of Farca and the likes, so if that's up your alley you'll most likely also enjoy this one.

Though: an unfortunate difference between those games and this one is both the depth & usage of the built in systems/tools at your disposal, the very linear story, and the playtime of the game. Starting with the latter, a normal playthrough of the game sits around 2 to 3 hours. As the game is very linear in terms of choices you can make (the choices only change a few minor responses, there is only a singular ending and your choices don't affect this) there is not really a great reason to replay the game unless you're going for all achievements; as some are missable on a first playthrough.

Which makes the price, +-14EUR (without sale, as of writing this), a complicated point.

Apart from the playtime, the game makes up for it by the amazing voice acting (not AI generated), _amazing_ polished look and feel (you can clearly see a lot of love and thought were poured into this) and really interesting scenes (artistic direction wise) splattered between days. All in all, really good experience and amazing opener; especially for an indie developer. (there are some minor complaints such as the chat stealing your focus when having to make a choice preventing you from typing in a different window, but nothing game breaking.) -- Just in the end wished with this much work & love put into it, the story was a tad longer.

My final gripe was the somewhat limited use and complexity of the tools given to you. It goes hand in hand with the point about playtime, because how else would you utilize a lab analysis tool or terminal if not by expanding the story. There were tools that looked really interesting, but are in the end just used once; which is a shame really. The times you do utilize them are fun and all feel unique.

So. All in all, a really solid game that I see more so as a foundation for something bigger. It at times feels more like a demo than an full game story wise. If you don't mind the price for what you're getting, and games like orwell are up your alley; you'll enjoy this one. But it may be better to wait for the operator 2 (which is currently in development!) or play a similar game if you're looking for a longer story or if you don't prefer the linear story style of this game.

[h1][b] TLDR: Sells itself as an investigative puzzler but delivers a mostly on-rails visual novel experience. The handful of genuine puzzles are great, making their scarcity all the more frustrating.
[/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
➕Neat investigative puzzles (ENHANCE….ENHANCE)
➕Some nice puzzles, like bomb defuse

[h1]NEUTRALS: [/h1]
🔹Story is good, but a bit too on-rails and hand-holding

[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖Lots of unskippable intentionally blurry cutscenes leaves a cheap or vague feeling
➖Some reveals are not as big as they should be simply because you wouldn’t know things that your character would know

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
The game world takes place entirely from a computer screen and is set in the 90s, we’re talking older CRT monitor screens. There’s not much exploration to be found, as you work for the government and everything is pretty locked down. I’d say the world is a bit basic and simple, only serving as a UI to show some puzzles. 

The narrative has some good parts. You play as Evan Tanner, a Federal Department of Investigation (FDI) operator, in which your job is to assist field agents. You very quickly learn that there’s something going on and you are enlisted, whether you want to or not, to uncover the truth. 
So while I did enjoy the story to an extent, any scene not at the computer and is told through a characters eyes is a blurry mess of objects that are nearly undecipherable. This could be something related to the story, but I don’t want to give the game the benefit of the doubt here and say that it worsens the experience. 

[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The gameplay seems pretty cool at first, but you quickly realize how on-rails the game is. Essentially, this is a glorified visual novel with a few puzzles sprinkled in. At first, I felt like Garcia from Criminal Minds - I was the internet sleuth assisting agents in the field by giving them on-the-fly information to help with cases. But unfortunately, the game isn’t as cool as that. 
The loop consists of you having a conversation, being presented with evidence, and then using the 2-3 tools at your disposal to answer a question presented by the conversation. For example, you’ll need to identify a killer and a victim by scanning their faces to get their names, then look them up in the FDI database. Same thing with licenses plates or analyzing footage/pictures. It does sound very cool, but I can’t emphasize enough the on-rails experience and lack of deep puzzle mechanics. This is more of a game focused on the narrative. 

The difficulty is forgiving. I’m pretty sure I made every wrong choice in the game, yet still made it to the end. I literally messed up a [spoiler]bomb defuse and got an agent killed[/spoiler]. Whoops. Despite these consequences, this doesn’t seem like it impacted the game as much and wasn’t mentioned again other than a few brief times after the fact. 

[h1] [b] Graphics (Quality/Technical) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Being that the game is from the point of view of a computer screen and all “Real” scenes are a blurry mess, I’d say the quality isn’t great. What footage you do see is grainy 90’s-era quality, but aside from that the computer UI is good and crisp. 

On the technical side, I had no issues, encountered no bugs, and ran the game without issues. 

1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSD  

[h1] [b] Audio – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The music isn’t really noticeable, but it does increase in intensity during high-drama parts. 

There is a lot of voice acting, and it all sounds good. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [2/10] [/b] [/h1]
Not a lot of replay value here, unless you want to redo the puzzles again for achievements. 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The Operator is described as a game with detective/investigation, and puzzle elements. I’d estimate the game to be about 70% story/narrative focus, 20% puzzles, and 10% deducing or investigating. I’d say that Operator is an okay game, but I was a bit disappointed by the mystery and investigative sides. This is very much a visual novel game more than anything, and as someone that likes visual novels, I was expecting more to use my brain to make deductions instead of clicking pre-defined replies. 

The game does have a few puzzles. I’d say maybe ~10 at the most, and despite that small number, I found them to be good puzzles. Analyzing gunpowder was really cool. Defusing a bomb on the fly was also great. If the game was more focused on gameplay like that, then I’d give it a much higher score, but these are the highest highs that The Operator offers, and there’s only a few of them. 

The real focus of the game is on the narrative. While I wouldn’t consider the narrative to be bad, there were a few parts that were either ridiculously obvious, or a missed opportunity. 
Obvious, because of metagaming - anyone who watches mystery shows knows that there’s only so many characters who could be the culprit due to you the show introducing them to the viewer. Same concept here, it’s obviously going to be the handful of people you know about already. 
Missed opportunity because you as the player only know what you know. One part in particular [spoiler]has the player finding out his apartment is being watched with a camera, and you have to identify whose apartment it is[/spoiler]. Well how can you possibly figure that out without knowing anything about the characters' life, nor ever having been there? Dumb. 

Overall, I do recommend The Operator, but it’s important that you know what you’re going into. This is NOT about deduction or investigating, and that’s not necessarily a bad thing, but I feel the game presents itself in a way that it’s something that it isn’t. 

[h1] [b] Recommend? (Price) [Y/N] [/b] [/h1]
[h1]Yes[/h1]
$14 base price is a bit much for a ~5 hour game with very low replay value. Wait for a sale. Around ~$5-7 would be a good point.

This is going to be the oddest negative review I have ever left. This game got me philosophical about reviews: Is a game review to describe whether I think the game is well made? Or is the game review to describe whether I enjoyed it? It's so rare that these two things are out of alignment, I wasn't sure what to write here. I have decided to write a review based on my enjoyment.

So let me just say: This game is well made. It is VERY well made. It's mechanics are a little bit "Papers, Please", a little bit "Clandestine", and a little bit "The Roottrees are Dead" - all meant as a compliment. The production values are top notch. And the story is very well written and very engaging.

And that's where the problem comes in. When a game is this good, my enjoyment hinges on the story being satisfying - and this story is FAR from satisfying. The ending is a cliffhanger that should have been the INTRODUCTION to a game, not a game in itself. And aside from being an incomplete story, the ending is nothing but [spoiler]bad things happening to good people and bad people getting away with it[/spoiler]. And I find that an extremely unsatisfying experience.

So I leave this review to convey an experience for people like me: people who can appreciate a masterfully crafted game that delivers a deeply unsatisfying story. If I'd known how the story ended, I wouldn't have bothered.

*Well made thriller, intriguing story, albeit flawed and very short*

The Operator has you play as Evan Tanner, the titular operator of the fictional FDI. Your task is to sit behind a computer and conduct forensic inestigations with state-of-the-art tools to help your colleagues in the field. 
You quickly become part of a major conspiracy and need to uncover the secrets of a series of missing cases and murders.

I did enjoy my time with the games but it has a fair amount of shortcomings, my main issues being the short length and abrupt ending.

The game mainly involves you getting sent files such as video feeds by FDI agents that you need to sleuth through to uncover important information such as the ID of a suspect. The tasks are pretty varied to keep it from getting stale. However, the game does not flesh out the gameplay. Many tasks are done only once, making it feel fairly shallow. 

The main focus is clearly the story. It is intriguing and does enough to keep you hooked. 
The voice actors do a good job portraying their characters, although they can feel underdeveloped. While I did enjoy it for the most part, it felt rushed to me. The already fast pacing picks up at the end, and then the game just ends, leaving many unanswered questions. The game also teases multiple endings by giving you the illusion of choices throughout the story, but there is only a singular storyline.

The presentation is well done and immersive thanks to the visuals and sound design. The soundtrack also does a good job accompanying the story by kicking in at important beats.

As I mentioned a few times, the game is overly short; you could probably beat it in three hours. For the story it's setting up, I feel like it'd need more time to tell it in full.

Overall, the Operator gets a slight recommend from me. But maybe wait for a discount for this one.

My experience with The Operator can be summed up as follows: great presentation, limited investigation.  It's a  game that looks sharp, feels polished, and tells a story that is rather entertaining, yet never quite trusts you enough to truly investigate it on your own. I enjoyed my time with it. I just kept wishing it would let me off the leash.

The production is slick from top to bottom. The performances sell the drama, and the narrative momentum keeps you moving even when a few plot holes start to peek through if you linger too long on the details. It is a fun story. It just is not a particularly demanding one.

Let’s be clear about something. This is not really an investigation game.

You are deliberately guided from one beat to the next with little room to wander or hope oiff the beaten path. That keeps the pacing tight, sure, but it also strips away the thrill of deduction that hallmarks great detective games . No alternate paths, no clever lateral thinking moments, no opportunities to feel like you outsmarted the system. Outside of one genuinely challenging, spoiler free sequence that actually made me pause and think, most of the puzzles feel straightforward and simple to resolve.

And then there is the ending. I assumed I had stumbled into the Bad Ending because of something I had done wrong, only to realize that this was simply... the finish. And I figured it was disappointing.

This game didn't scratch my detective game itch. I love having my detective instincts tested. I enjoy piecing together clues and trusting my logic to guide me. I wanted more depth, more resistance. That said, for someone easing into detective style games for the first time, this is an excellent starting point. As long as you're picking it up on sale.

The Operator, developed by Bureau 81 and published by Bureau 81 together with indienova, is a tightly focused narrative puzzle game that transforms the quiet, procedural work of intelligence analysis into a tense and engaging thriller. Rather than placing players in the role of an action hero or field agent, the game casts them as a desk-bound operator, someone whose power comes not from physical presence but from information, observation, and deduction. This shift in perspective defines the entire experience, creating a game that feels intimate, cerebral, and deliberately restrained.

You play as Evan Tanner, a newly recruited operator working for the fictional Federal Department of Intelligence. Your job is to support agents in the field by analysing data, processing evidence, and drawing connections that others might miss. The game unfolds almost entirely through Evan’s workstation, presented as a simulated computer desktop filled with databases, analysis tools, messaging systems, and case files. This interface-driven approach immediately sets the tone: instead of cinematic spectacle, The Operator relies on immersion through routine, making the player feel like they are genuinely sitting at a government terminal late at night, piecing together fragments of truth.

Gameplay revolves around solving a series of cases that gradually escalate in complexity and importance. Early tasks feel procedural—identifying suspects, tracing movements, or cross-referencing records—but as the story unfolds, patterns begin to emerge and the stakes rise. Players are required to closely read documents, examine photos and videos, search databases, and interpret subtle clues hidden in plain sight. The puzzles reward attentiveness and logical reasoning, often asking players to synthesize information from multiple sources rather than relying on a single obvious answer. When a breakthrough occurs, it feels earned, the result of careful thought rather than trial and error.

As the narrative progresses, the game shifts from isolated casework into a broader conspiracy. A mysterious hacker begins to interfere with FDI systems, raising questions about surveillance, authority, and the reliability of the information you’re working with. This transition adds narrative tension without abandoning the game’s grounded tone. The story remains largely linear, but it is effectively paced, allowing suspense to build gradually as seemingly unrelated assignments reveal deeper connections. Dialogue and character interactions are understated, delivered through calls, messages, and system prompts rather than dramatic cutscenes, which reinforces the feeling that you are always working behind the scenes.

One of the game’s greatest strengths is how convincingly it uses its interface as both a storytelling and gameplay tool. Every window, search bar, and analysis program feels purposeful, and learning how to use these tools becomes part of the experience. While some mechanics are simplified or exaggerated for gameplay purposes, they remain believable within the fiction, maintaining immersion. The design encourages players to slow down, double-check assumptions, and think critically—mistakes often stem from overlooking details rather than misunderstanding mechanics.

Visually, The Operator embraces a minimalist, utilitarian aesthetic inspired by older operating systems and institutional software. The interface is dense but readable, intentionally lacking visual flair in favor of authenticity. This design choice may feel dry to some players, but it suits the game’s themes perfectly, emphasizing bureaucracy, control, and the monotony of surveillance work. Subtle audio cues, ambient hums, and restrained music enhance tension without distracting from concentration, allowing the player’s focus to remain on the task at hand.

In terms of pacing, the game strikes a careful balance. It is compact, typically completed in a handful of hours, but it avoids feeling rushed. Each case builds naturally on the last, and the increasing narrative weight keeps momentum strong. The linear structure limits replayability, as choices rarely branch into significantly different outcomes, but this also allows the developers to maintain tight narrative control and deliver a coherent, focused story without filler.

Community reception reflects appreciation for the game’s originality and execution. Players who enjoy detective work, mystery narratives, and “games on a computer” style experiences frequently praise its atmosphere and puzzle design. Criticism tends to focus on its short length, limited player agency, and occasional moments where immersion is broken by game-like constraints. Even so, these issues rarely overshadow the strengths of the experience, particularly for players aligned with its intended audience.

Taken as a whole, The Operator is a confident and distinctive narrative puzzle game that finds tension in observation rather than action. It succeeds by committing fully to its premise, turning data analysis and desk work into compelling gameplay through thoughtful design and strong thematic focus. While it may not appeal to players seeking open-ended systems or high replay value, it offers a memorable, tightly constructed experience for those who enjoy slow-burn storytelling, logical deduction, and the quiet unease of uncovering truths from behind a screen.

The Operator – 8/10 – A Tense and Captivating Dive into Espionage

The Operator is a stealth-driven, psychological thriller that plunges players into the shadowy world of covert operations, high-stakes intelligence, and moral ambiguity. With an engaging narrative and a compelling atmosphere, it combines tactical gameplay with deep narrative exploration, offering a gripping experience for fans of espionage games. While it may not reinvent the wheel, The Operator does a great job of delivering a tightly-paced, immersive story that keeps you on the edge of your seat.

In The Operator, you play as a field agent working for a secretive government agency, tasked with handling covert missions that blur the lines between right and wrong. The game is heavy on stealth and strategy, as you navigate through a series of complex scenarios—whether infiltrating a heavily guarded facility, gathering intelligence, or neutralizing a threat. The gameplay is tense and slow-paced, with an emphasis on thinking ahead, blending in with your surroundings, and making choices that can lead to either success or failure. It’s all about staying unseen, listening for clues, and using your limited resources wisely. The tension constantly builds as you wonder if you’ll be caught or if the consequences of your decisions will haunt you later on.

The game’s mechanics are simple but effective. You don’t have a full arsenal at your disposal like in many action-heavy titles, and that’s part of the charm. The focus here is on patience, strategy, and managing the few tools you have, whether it’s a silenced pistol or hacking equipment. The difficulty comes not from constant firefights but from the challenge of navigating through dangerous environments, avoiding detection, and managing the relationships and choices you make along the way.

One of The Operator’s strongest points is its atmosphere. The game does an excellent job of crafting a sense of isolation and tension, using sound design, lighting, and environment to its advantage. The dark, minimalist environments add to the oppressive mood, and the voice acting and soundtrack complement the sense of secrecy and paranoia that runs throughout the game. You always feel like you’re being watched, and every decision could push you deeper into the world of shadowy operatives and untrustworthy allies.

The narrative is intriguing and filled with twists, as you’ll often have to decide whether to follow orders or act according to your own moral compass. The story doesn’t just follow the usual espionage tropes—it explores themes of trust, betrayal, and the emotional toll of being part of a covert operation. The characters you meet, especially the ones you interact with the most, are well-written and add layers of complexity to the plot. The game gives you enough room to shape your own interpretation of events, but it doesn’t shy away from showing the darker consequences of a life lived in secrecy.

However, The Operator does have its shortcomings. The stealth mechanics, while solid, can feel repetitive at times, especially in the later levels where the pacing slows down significantly. There are also a few technical hiccups, like occasional AI pathfinding issues or moments when the game’s visuals don’t quite match the level of detail of the environments. Some players may also find the slower pace a bit tedious, particularly if they’re expecting a more action-packed experience.

8/10 – A Solid, Tense Espionage Experience
The Operator is a highly effective stealth game that delivers a tense, engaging experience for anyone who loves espionage narratives. While its mechanics might feel repetitive in certain sections, the atmosphere, story, and the moral complexity of the choices you make keep it captivating throughout. The game’s slow pace and emphasis on stealth give it a unique edge in a genre often dominated by faster-paced action. If you’re a fan of games that require patience and strategic thinking, The Operator will keep you hooked. It might not be perfect, but it’s a well-executed, atmospheric title that leaves a lasting impression.

I didn't know what to expect going into this game and 2 days later, waiting eagerly for a sequel.

EDIT: I've been thinking about this a lot, and I just wanted to add one more thing. You can see how I go into quite a bit of initial, just-coming-down-off-finishing-the-game detail down below if you'd like, but I'd like to quickly say here, at the start, that I think a big part of the issue was a fundamental misunderstanding of what this game was. I went into this expecting a puzzle game, but it isn't so much a puzzle game as it is a story game.
I feel it's advertised as more of a puzzle game with subtle hints at an overarching story you might be able to uncover, and indeed it does *play* like a puzzle game... until it very much becomes about following the narrative.
My feelings below still stand - including the ones after my spoiler tags - but while I don't know that I would've felt *differently* if I'd gone into this expecting something different, much of my confusion and disappointment might've been at least softened.

ORIGINAL REVIEW:
Overall, I was pretty disappointed with this game.
First, it was incredibly short - I had the game open for 7-ish hours... but I had dinner, fed the dogs, took a shower, yada yada, with it paused, so I'm not actually sure how long it really took. Most of the puzzles themselves weren't particularly challenging - though the mechanics were satisfying in a point-and-click, ASMR kind of way - and then one or two of the puzzles were SUPER, out-of-pocket complicated, insanely difficult, and totally out of place?? And because of the length of the game, I felt like all the mechanics I was learning, I really didn't need for very long, or often even more than once.
The writing, acting, sound design, and off-screen auditory storytelling were beautiful. Very well done; you can tell a lot of love went into it, there just... wasn't a whole lot of content.

I saw someone mention that if there were an "operator mode," that would make up for a lot of this problem, and I agree. *MILD SPOILER* Every single one of the cases were directly linked to the main story, and I think being able to enjoy some of the mechanics for longer would make it feel a little more worthwhile. Again, many of the puzzles were fairly simple, but it was still fun and satisfying in a way, and then it would also be more impactful - learning how to do the more complicated puzzles - because you'd have to use that knowledge again.

**SPOILERS FOR THE END**

The ending was incredibly dissatisfying to me. I immediately got off and looked to see if I somehow got "the bad ending" and there was another way I could've played to get "the good ending," but no. It is what it is - one and done. (I saw someone else say that if there HAD been multiple endings, that would also help with the overarching "the game is too short" issue everyone seems to be having, and I agree with that, as well.)
Some people liked the ending, but a lot of people shared the same feelings I have: if I uncover the mystery, am taking notes on the story and correctly piecing together the clues, I want to feel like I 'won' the video game... at least to a degree. But (again, **HUGE SPOILER AHEAD**) it literally doesn't matter at all. Nothing you did, none of the choices you made, mattered. The main character you played dies, every SINGLE one of your contacts/friends dies or goes missing (you cannot save them, it does not matter, and you're informed of their demise in during-credits news clippings, no less), and the only one to escape is HAL, and they're still trying to take down the big bad 30 years later (which is what fans of the ending consider the "silver lining.")
I love when games do some out-of-the-box stuff, but the whole game sets you up like you're uncovering a mystery, exposing a story, and then in the end literally not a lick of it mattered (except that HAL escaped and is still trying, which as far as I can tell, happens no matter what you, as the player, do.) It just felt very forced, and pretty pointless.
Disappointing, because again, some of the mechanics were really neat, and you can tell a lot of love was put into the storytelling aspects.

I am kinda torn about this game since what is there is not necessarily bad  but ... people should know what they are getting into.

Its sad because the system that are there could have been incredible for solving more complicated cases but unfortunately the entire game is basically a tutorial where people always tell you what to do and there is very little to figure out.

Next the story: Unfortunately if you pay attention to the clues the game gives you you will figure out 90% of the plotbeats before the game tells you and its pretty akward when the game treats something as a relvelation you basically knew for quite a while already.

The story is also linear it might seem you can pick sides but ultimately there is only one direction to go. Another thing is that the ending  is ... well its difficult to say much without spoiling but its pretty dark and for me put a pretty big damper on everything that happened.

I would not say the game is worth full price to be honest maybe on a deep discount. Only buy if you are looking for an interactive story more than a detective/puzzle game.

Well, in this game all you do is type and click, but it didn't get boring at all and nothing really felt repetitive. Some tasks like the chemical analysis and the bomb were really unique, made me wish it wasn't just a one time thing. Even the normal "scan face, look up criminal, send their name" tasks were quite fun. I'm not the sharpest and usually spam the hint button in these type of games, despite this I only asked for help once trying to find a certain badge for a code. The puzzles make you think, but not frustrate you with their complexity.
 
There were two things that I didn't like at all in this game, one being the ending. Even though I did everything right, I still got the bad ending with no satisfying end. The other problem being the big plot twist. As soon as I heard about the COLE family, combined with the files with the 100 names, and the intro cutscene, I basically already knew what the great reveal was going to be. It should've been hidden better, at least until the research facility part of the story.
 
Finally, I do wish there was more build up, that you complete some "filler" tasks before the whole conspiracy story begins. The progression felt a bit too fast for my taste, I would've enjoyed getting a few calls from agents who ask for help, not related to the story. Still this is one of those games where the story hooked me so bad I wished there was a movie of it. Definitely buying the sequal as soon as it's released.

The graphics are really good, and the way the game plays, it's one of the smoothest things ever. Even considering the fact that this game doesn't even take up much of your space. The story is top notch. The plot twist (especally near the end) are one of the craziest things I heard inside of a video game. It also just really fun to play with all the character interactions and the before mentioned smooth gameplay.

The voice acting was preformed really well by everyone who played a role, and made me feel like I was in the actual world of the game. But the lines for this game could be a bit cheesy, but most of it is fine.

There are also so many sections of this game that have you on the edge of your seat, and it's cool to see each little detail mentioned into this big mystery. 

The puzzles are perfect, it's not too hard to understand, but it's also not to easy to get immediantly. Sometimes when you finish a puzzle you feel like Albert Einstin. Also stay for the credits, those last second details made my jaw drop.

Cons:

Because I liked the game sooo much, I was disapointed that it was quite frankly a pretty short game. The game also ends on a very high note, which left me iching for more. Like, you can buy the game, finish it, and barly return it for a refund (but don't do that, support the devs).

This game, although great, is not worth 17 bucks. The main reason being because of it's short story, if you want to get this game, I suggest wishlisting and waiting for a sale.

I really enjoyed my time with The Operator, but I finished it feeling like I’d only played the first episode of a much larger game.

The story is genuinely good and kept me engaged the whole way through. Some of the plot twists are fairly predictable, but there are a few moments that genuinely caught me off guard. The problem is that just as things start to really open up… it ends. My first playthrough took around 2 hours, with maybe another hour for a second run to clean up missed achievements.

Where the game really shines is the audio. The music and sound design are fantastic, especially how the soundtrack and effects subtly shift when you uncover something important. Those moments feel great and add a lot of tension. The voice acting across the board is also strong, making the characters feel believable despite the minimal presentation.

Gameplay-wise, I had a lot of fun. There are loads of small, varied “puzzles” that all work in different ways — digging through databases, connecting information, spotting inconsistencies. Nothing ever feels repetitive, but at the same time, many mechanics are introduced, used once, and then never expanded on. It feels like groundwork being laid for systems that never get the chance to evolve.

Overall, this is a great game and absolutely worth picking up on sale to kill a few hours. At its current price point, though, it feels like it’s missing crucial length. The biggest issue is that it feels like the beginning of a story with no ending, rather than a complete experience.

I don’t regret playing it — I just wish there was more of it.

I would classify this as a short narrative game with very light puzzles.

PUZZLES
A majority of the puzzles are signposted and obvious, and they all give a tutorial vibe. The game will teach you how to solve a particular type of puzzle, but then that type of puzzle is never visited again.

There were two puzzles that weren't, but these felt frustrating as:
- the first one had VERY confusing wording and used terms that were not explained ("tickable" being the word I got stuck on)
- the second one you needed to brute force a solution, which is never fun nor rewarding

NARRATIVE
For a mystery game, the final twist was basically shouted at the beginning of the game and I guessed it within the first 5 minutes. All of the cases pertain to the main mystery (no side missions to divert your attention). When you know the secret right away, it's hard to feel motivated to continue playing.

In the end, I felt it was a shallow, predictable, and simple game. It has good bones, but needed a lot more time in the oven

If a sequel does come along, or this team makes a similar game, I hope they:
- Include more puzzles
- Not make the ending obvious
- Playtest all the puzzles to make sure that things are easily understood and enjoyable (without losing the theme)
- Add in some red herrings/busywork 
- Show off their systems! Similar to a Hypnospace Outlaw or The Roottrees are Dead, have us use the mechanics more than once before moving on to a completely different thing. I would have loved to do more searching, scrubbing, etc in the game but didn't have enough opportunities outside each mechanic's single puzzle.

[h1]The Operator – Review[/h1]
I’ve just finished my first playthrough of [i]The Operator[/i], and it really got under my skin. At first, it feels like a clear throwback to [i]Orwell[/i] — digging through files, connecting clues, and sitting with that constant, uneasy sense of surveillance. The retro desktop setup is spot-on and makes the whole thing feel strangely real. About halfway through, I started wondering if the game itself was testing me. Was I part of the experiment? That thought stuck with me right to the end. The puzzles are clever and rewarding, and the story ramps up quickly, leaving you with plenty to think about. I’m already planning another run to see what I missed.

[hr][/hr]
[h2]What Holds It Back[/h2]
That said, the biggest drawback is its length. At around three to four hours, it ends just as you’re fully immersed. I couldn’t help but think how much more replayable it could be with a few extra systems layered on top.
[list]
[*]Randomised agents
[*]Modular or shuffled case fragments
[*]Overlapping investigative threads across multiple cases
[/list]
Something like that would fit perfectly with the game’s investigative tone and make it feel less like a one-and-done experience. Piecing together evidence that changes each run would add a lot of longevity.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Similar Games Worth Mentioning[/h2]
If you enjoyed [i]Orwell[/i] or [i]Her Story[/i], you’ll feel right at home here. That said, if you’re looking for longer playtime, there are other options worth considering:
[list]
[*][b]Orwell[/b] – branching choices across multiple episodes
[*][b]Return of the Obra Dinn[/b] – a sprawling mystery with dozens of characters
[*][b]The Case of the Golden Idol[/b] – interconnected cases with deep logic puzzles
[*][b]Cyber Manhunt[/b] – hacking and social engineering-driven investigations
[*][b]Shadows of Doubt[/b] – a procedural detective sandbox with near-infinite replayability
[/list]
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]
This is a short, sharp, and stylish thriller that absolutely nails its atmosphere and narrative hooks. It’s not perfect — some dialogue feels stiff, and the illusion of choice can occasionally be frustrating — but for a few hours of tense, thought‑provoking gameplay, it’s absolutely worth it. I just hope a possible sequel takes the next step and gives us the freedom to dig deeper, for longer.

[b]Recommendation:[/b] [u]Recommended[/u]

You are Evan Tanner, an FBI Operator, assisting field agents by searching through files and coordinating stuff. Your first case is a murder where a man named Jenkins was shot, and a list with a bunch of names is found. The weird thing: one of the names was censored, but only after the document got secured as evidence, so theres some shady cover-up shit happening inside of the FBI.
Then, you get contacted by HAL (Alice Truman), a wanted hacker, who needs your help with uncovering said shady shit. Later, Jenkins killer gets shot by a mysterious bold man who is in no database.

A bunch of shit happens, and you find out about a biomedical company named BioM, lead by Jenkins, whose target it is to create a drug that can erase memories. Jenkins intention is to make it possible to erase trauma from peoples memories (his daughter (probably) took her life because she got traumatized or something idk and then his wife killed herself as well...). However, the funding comes from some shadow-world-government people who intend to use the drug to erase peoples minds and rewrite their memories. Spoiler: You are one of those. You are a double agent, sent to win HALs trust. But you don't know that, since your objective is deeply burried inside of your mind.
In the end, you and HAL (and some others) try to find out who the double-agent in the FBI is by infiltrating the server room. However, the hitman from earlier, who got caught at some point in the story (irrelevant) is freed by said double-agent and shoots some people. You try to escapa but get shot. Everything is covered up as you being the double-agent (which si partially true because you ARE one, but not THE one) and all your friends get shot or jailed. HAL, who gives you her identity, is compromised since you ,remeber, are a double agent, so you somehow redirect that information to the hitman guy or the shadow government or idk who the fuck but basically it was all a huge trap to infiltrate the possible resistance that could pose a threat to said shadow government. You and all your friends die and all of your actions were meaningless. THE END.

Avoid if you want to play a game with a minimum of agency.

Now for my main issue: This game is way too short for the price. The game took me 4 hours and that was without trying to go fast. If I tried I feel like this game could be 100% in less that 3 hours (maybe even <2h).

Another issue is that it's very linear. It doesn't matter what you do, there is only a single ending. The different options only affect which 10 second response you'll get and nothing after that.

I don't think it's worth getting this game for the full price, but if it's for sale for <$10 it's an alright deal.

A Thriller That Rekindled My Creative Spark

🖥️ 🔍 ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆
🕹️ Great on Steam Deck

One of the reasons I became a software developer was the dream of eventually making games. Over the years, there have only been a handful of titles that truly reignited that spark and made game development feel possible again. The Operator unexpectedly became one of those games.

From its presentation to its atmosphere, the game pulled me in quickly, but it was the storytelling, especially toward the final stretch, that really hit. The ending was a genuine chef’s kiss. Not because it wrapped everything neatly, but because it didn’t. When it was over, I felt that familiar disappointment that only comes from wanting more. More answers about HAL. More about The Ghost. More about the Organization and where this world could go next.

I understand why some players felt like they were simply going through the motions to push the story forward. For me, curiosity carried the experience. I wanted to poke at every decision, even knowing the branching paths were not especially deep or wide. The choices still felt meaningful enough to keep me engaged and questioning the outcome.

If you’re looking for a short, focused thriller with an intriguing premise, believable characters, and a strong audiovisual presentation, The Operator is absolutely worth your time. Especially on sale. It’s the kind of game that lingers in your head after the credits roll, and quietly nudges your creative mind into motion.

The Operator offers a remarkably engaging narrative experience, supported by a strong storyline and a well-executed plot twist. The structure of each case is thoughtfully designed: from the call system to the investigative tasks, every step feels purposeful and polished. Working through evidence, analyzing data, and piecing together conclusions is consistently satisfying and stands out as one of the game’s greatest strengths.

Because the investigative tools and the workstation interface are so enjoyable to use, I found myself wishing for a mode that would provide long-term engagement beyond the main story. The campaign can be completed relatively quickly, and once it ends, the gameplay loop—despite being excellent—comes to an abrupt stop.

A dedicated free-play or “ongoing operations” mode could meaningfully extend the game’s lifespan. For example, players could receive procedurally generated cases or scenario-based assignments that scale in complexity, allowing them to continue applying the tools and systems introduced in the main storyline. This would give players who enjoy the investigative process a space to keep refining their skills and exploring the mechanics without a fixed ending.

I am very much looking forward to The Operator 2, and I genuinely believe that adding an optional long-term mode—whether free-play, case generator, or rotating scenario board—would significantly enhance replay value and increase the game’s overall appeal.

For anyone considering this title: the core experience is absolutely worth it, and the investigative gameplay is exceptionally well-crafted. The story alone justifies the €14 price, and I can recommend it without hesitation.

I wanted to love this game but I just cannot recommend you spend money on what is ultimately a disappointing experience. 

The game has a great concept with a strong atmosphere, and what I hoped was great potential but the overall experience ends up feeling disappointingly thin. Reading reviews and looking at the blurb I felt that I was promised tension, deduction, and deeper problem-solving. Unfortunately, it never fully delivers on that potential.

The biggest issue is simply its length. Just as the mechanics start to click and the world begins to feel intriguing, the game is over. It ends before it can build momentum or explore its own ideas in any meaningful way. What could have been a gripping investigation feels more like the prologue to a larger game that never arrives.

The story also ends up predictable. Key beats begin to telegraph themselves early, and the ending lands exactly where you expect it to. Without twists, red herrings, or layers to peel back, the narrative lacks the depth needed to keep you engaged or surprised.

The investigations themselves feel shallow as well. Each case presents a problem, but they’re often solved with just a few simple steps. There’s rarely a need to dig deeper, only once or twice was I cross-referencing clues, or genuinely thinking like an investigator. Instead of complex puzzles or branching deductions, you get straightforward tasks that resolve too quickly to be satisfying.

Overall, The Operator is an interesting idea wrapped in a very short, very predictable package. If you’re looking for a brief atmospheric diversion, it works—but if you want a substantial investigative experience, this one doesn’t reach far enough.

Things to know: 

1: The story is linear. However, it's a good story, so you won't really care.
2: No re-playability (unless you really want to just grab any achievement you may have missed, but otherwise no point to playing it more than once) . However, not all games need re-playability to be fully worth the cost. 
3: it is a short game. it took me about 4 hours to beat it and that was me taking my time and looking at everything. 

Summary: in this game, you feel as though you are playing a main role in a cat and mouse police thriller movie. It is NOT horror, but it IS suspenseful.  And when I say playing a character in a movie-I mean just that. not playing a character in a game like a movie, but a real "This is you, this is your job, this is what you are having to face" feel to it that really pulls you in. While the main plot isn't unique, the slight twists especially at the very end and the variations they used to tell this main story make it a stand out game.  if you loved movies like face off or silences of the lambs or anything along those lines, you absolutely will enjoy this game. cheaper than going to an actual movie theatre  and for something that will last you twice as long as a standard movie.  

This is definitely one of the best games of this style I have ever seen or played, and i highly recommend it. given some of the puzzles, I would say this game is definitely better suited to adult gamers, but anyone with the intelligence and patience for such things would probably really enjoy this IF they enjoy cat and mouse thriller movies.  

Also as a bonus: Due to the style it is made in, you do NOT need a top of the line computer or anywhere near close to it to play it. So if you have a dirt cheap PC from say the last 5 years?  Chances are it will run absolutely fine and with no need to change any settings. I am running on a rig almost 3 generations behind at this point, and had zero issues with this game. 

It also looks like the developers are working on a sequel to this game. Unknown if that will continue further into this story or be a new one entirely, but if they  keep the save high level of story telling and suspense I have no doubt it will also be amazing.   

I honestly didn't have to many hopes when going into this game, but for once I was absolutely amazed at what I actually got. So if you can get it either at full price or on sale, I definitely recommend it. just don't go into it thinking its going to be a hundreds of hours or infinite re-playability game and you should have no problems either.

It's an interesting game and I enjoyed playing a bit of it, but the developer has a specific idea in mind about how it is to be played and I'm not into that.  Specifically, when listening to an audio file, the controls are locked and you can't do anything else.  The developer has said that he wants to be able to focus the player's attention, but that's not how my attention works and it's very uncomfortable.  Instead of focusing my intention, it's like someone powered up a megaphone next to my ear and is shouting, "this is all artificial!  Stop being immersed!  This is a video game!  The stakes are very low because none of this is real!"

The ideal situation for me would be being able to replay all of the audios - including recordings of the "real time" conversations - repeatedly while I peruse the visual and text data.  This is how I have investigated things in the past (though those were technical investigations and not criminal investigations): get everything in front of me and let my mind chew on a bunch of it at once to get into it.

I'm not exactly normal when it comes to my focus and attention, but the make or break question for Steam reviews is, "would I recommend this?"  In this case, I don't.

UPDATE: I'm not suggesting that the dev should change the game to suit me; I'm just saying that I don't recommend it.

I really enjoyed the style of investigation and the way the story was unfolding piece by piece. However, the ending fell flat and painted my overall opinion as negative. None of your actions mattered in any shape or form, there is really only one ending to be had. The choices are just an illusion, all paths lead to the same end. I guess some people like it, but for me this immediately detached all the emotion I had invested to the game and the characters and it felt like I had waisted all that time trying to choose the right path. 

A lot of strings were also left loose, and while it may have been to tease a sequel, it did not feel satisfying. A good game should be it's own complete piece that can enjoyed without digging through a Discord server for additional info or waiting for a sequel to explain everything. 

Another grievance I have with the game lies in the save system; you can't manually save and it only happens automatically at certain checkpoints. This feels extremely outdated and forces you to either play for an unknown amount of time until you hit a checkpoint, or you have to keep starting the day over because your progress isn't saved. Just give people the option to save manually and reload from a checkpoint if they have forgotten what happened. I had to take a 10 month break from the game because the save system made playing feel like a chore - you can't just play for a few minutes (or however long you feel like playing) at a time because your progress could be all for nothing.

I think the game and the developer have a lot of potential and I believe that if the second game fixes all these issues, it can be GREAT.

--- BUY THIS GAME WHEN IT IS ON SALE ---

I paid ~ $13.00 and that is TOO much for this game. I think a fair price for this game is $5.00 due to play hours and lack of replayability.

PROs:

+ I like investigative puzzle games and this one was intriguing.
+ Story was compelling.
+ I liked the idea of using different systems to discover information and link said information together.
+ I am looking forward to a sequel. Hopefully it will be longer than this game.

CONs:

- I beat it twice in 7 hours so average game play time was 3.5 hours. I really only played it twice to get the achievements though.
     - I don't think the price of the game should be this high for such a short game. Especially since there isn't a lot of replayability with this game :/.
- The story gives the illusion of choice but regardless of dialogue options, you still end up where you are intended to go; very RAILROADY
- The game has investigative tools but for most of them you only use them once throughout the entire game.
- For my second playthrough, I was REALLY wanting a skip button for scenes where the protagonist "goes home at the end of the day;" It was really boring to sit through those scenes.
- There are some locked files that you don't get access to, which was disappointing. There were many missed opportunities to build lore or give players opportunities to poke around, even if they resulted in dead ends, it would have been nice to fill out the world a little more.
- It would have been nice if there was a reward/punishment system for being smart or needing to have your hand held through the whole game. Some sort of variable input that would impact the game based on player actions. Like a trust meter so if people trust you, it is easier to lie to them or something.

I know it sounds like I am taking a huge dump on this game but my goal is to help the developers with the sequel.The game has A LOT of good ideas, I just think the execution and the offering could have been better.

That being said, I liked the game and I want to see more from this developer.

What makes this game even more disturbing is that it purposely references events that actually happened. Back in the 50s and 60s, CIA was responsible for several illegal experiments on people without their consent for "military purposes" under [b]Project MKUltra[/b], just like in the game... dosing them with drugs, conducting harsh interviews, and trying to implant false memories or break down minds for their own purpose, and even using all the UFO sightings events to misdirect attention and hide all that bs. [i]The Operator[/i] captures that exact atmosphere: the manipulation, the paranoia, the feeling that even your own thoughts might not be yours.

Aesthetically pleasing, good story with at the very least, decent voice acting if not great. Runs well. An interesting gameplay mechanic that has you sitting at your desk, putting together pieces of the puzzles as agents sweep the field for evidence and follow the leads you help develop. The story has you unraveling a conspiracy, using computer tools, metadata, and analyzing software to pull the narrative together. It's fascinating, and the game does a really good job at making you feel like you're truly a professional analyst, solving crimes from the comfort of a desk in Washington DC.

Problem is, the game is pretty darn short. Only about 4 hours of gameplay, and it feels deeply on rails, to the point that the puzzle portion of it feels more like a addon to the rest of the game. If you subscribe to the $1 per hour mindset, even discounted to $9, this game is technically not worth it, as the game has limited replayability. Though, the game does make up for it with the story and gameplay to a degree. It is, at the very least, a pretty impactful 4 hours, and you could get somewhat different results if you repeat the story, so there is a small sense that your choices matter. 

I might just be spoiled, coming off of The Roottrees are Dead which had a fairly similar premise of using a computer to uncover information that can fill in the blanks. But in TRaD, they introduce you to the tools and then you spend a bulk of the time using them on your own to fill in profiles on the family tree. There was a lot more blanks to fill in and time to spend fiddling around with information. With TO, you get introduced to cool mechanics and tools on your computer, and then use almost none of them ever again. The game feels like a 4 hour tutorial other than the story, which takes interesting turns and, as a flipside, keeps the player continously faced with new and interesting problems to solve. It sucks not being able to repeatedly use a mechanic I got familiar with or a handbook I just learned, but every in-game day pulls me straight in with a curveball, gameplay wise or story wise.

The ending kinda left a bad taste in my mouth. AFAIK, your choices don't really seem to affect the ending from what I saw online in guides and gameplay.

Still gonna leave it as a positive review, because I quite enjoyed this and I think the devs are absolutely cooking here. I just hope the developers consider putting more meat on the bones of TO2, because it feels like there is a ton of potential for a truly great puzzle/detective game here that only gets partially realized.

"Finally, a game where I can live my dream of working in a government office"

Sit at a desk. Click through files. Listen to awkward phone calls. Welcome to The Operator, where being nosy is not only allowed—it’s the whole job.

No jumpscares, no monsters, just you and a pile of cases that slowly get weirder (in a good way). Somehow, it makes digging through reports and audio logs actually fun. The twists are smart, the vibe is chill, and you’ll feel like a genius when you piece things together—until the game reminds you you're not.

I absolutely loved The Operator. From the moment I stepped into Evan Tanner’s shoes, booting up that simulated desktop and diving into the role of a rookie operator at the Federal Department of Intelligence, I was hooked. The game didn’t just pull me into its world—it immersed me in a labyrinth of conspiracies, moral dilemmas, and surveillance, all wrapped in a retro ‘90s aesthetic with tech that felt eerily futuristic. It was nostalgic, yes, but also unsettling in the best way.

The gameplay was simple on the surface, but each task—analyzing grainy footage, cross-referencing databases, solving puzzles—made me feel like a true digital detective. It reminded me of Her Story, but stood firmly on its own legs with a tighter narrative and a mystery that grew darker and more complex with every click. The writing was spot-on, and the voice acting had a realism that drew me even deeper into the cases.

Honestly, my biggest gripe was that it ended too soon. I finished it in just a few hours, and while every minute was satisfying, I found myself wishing for more—more time in that richly constructed world, more twists, more layers. The cliffhanger at the end didn’t just tease a continuation; it practically begged for one. I’m really hoping Bureau 81 brings us a sequel that picks up right where the story left off.

Short as it was, The Operator delivered one of the most engaging and rewarding detective experiences I’ve played in ages. It made me pay attention, think critically, and trust my instincts. And I’d jump at the chance to return to that world the moment a sequel drops.

Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 98:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆☆ (8/10)

[i] The Operator [/i] casts you not as a hero in the field, but as the analyst—the voice behind the computer—supporting agents from the shadows. It’s a fascinating setup and a fresh twist on crime-solving games, and usually almost always lives up to its potential!

🖥[b] Pros: [/b]
[list]
[*] Authentic "operator" fantasy. You monitor missions from your desk, field phone calls, look through mysterious documents, and scrub through CCTV footage. 

[*] Diverse tools. The game gives you a chem scanner, facial recognition database, image enhancement tech, and document search systems. For example, in one mission, you identify a suspect by cross-referencing a blurry security camera with an equally blurry security footage of his car and license plate. That kind of detective work feels cool. You feel smart when it works.

[*] Great use of puzzles under pressure. A standout moment has you guiding a field agent through bomb defusal. You have to analyze chemicals, check your reference files, and read out step-by-step instructions—all while the timer ticks down. These time-sensitive missions are where the game shines.

[*] Well-done audio design. The UI clicks, radio static, and phone calls all contribute to a grounded, late-'90s thriller vibe. The voice acting is low-key but sells the scenario well, especially during moments of stress or confusion.

[*] No filler. It’s tight and focused. No wandering, no padding. You’re thrown into the action quickly and missions move at a brisk pace.
[/list]

[b]🧾 Cons: [/b]
[list]
[*] Flat characters. The field agents and mysterious hacker HAL are more archetypes than flesh-and-blood. They push the story forward, but rarely surprise

[*] Choices don’t matter much. There are dialogue branches, but most are cosmetic. Whether you’re professional or snarky, or even whether you succeed or fail at certain puzzles, the game mostly funnels you into the same story beats.

[*] Abrupt ending. The game ends just as things get interesting. HAL’s storyline ramps up, then vanishes. You barely get to dig into the conspiracy or see the consequences of your actions. It feels like a miniseries that ends on episode three.
[/list]

Hello developers,

 [spoiler]

During my play through, I tried to deliberately not answer the supervisor's calls or even pretended to be a 'good kid' to see if there was a way to betray HAL. But the game didn't give me any more options. I believe that in an interactive story game, player choices and their consequences are its true charm and what keeps players engaged.
The bomb disposal segment really stood out. I felt a strong sense of immersion and genuinely enjoyed being able to help someone. It's a shame that, probably due to the game's length, such a brilliant sequence only happened once.
The core puzzle was very cleverly designed, and its reveal was absolutely an adrenaline rush. I completely understand what you, as developers, wanted players to feel with that ending—the horror, the profound sense of melancholy, the sadness for the characters, and the lingering regret that a bigger enemy wasn't truly dealt with. However, even after experiencing all that, I still wished players could help the characters achieve a good ending. I truly love these characters.
Overall, this is a fantastic game! I really hope to play more from you in the future!

The Operator is a short but sweet game about assisting "FBI" agents while on cases, and uncovering a deeper conspiracy. 

The main gameplay is a mix of investigating cases using your FBI database and tools, and spotting contradicting parts of evidence. I enjoyed both the gameplay and the plot, and recommend this for anyone that thinks they would be interested.

Cons:

* The bomb defusal mission is just nonsensical. While it's obviously designed and written to be deliberately confusing to challenge the player, it is also ridiculous. The supervisor, Skinner, would be handling this, or at least offering assistance, not just casually leaving another agent's life up to a 3rd day employee who is reading the bomb defusal manual for the first time. Was having a good time in the game up until this mission. If you look at this achievement as well, only some ~50% of players have this achievement, and then you have to wonder, of those 50% how many had to look up a walk-through online in order to complete it? 
* Game was definitely somewhat dry at times where I felt a little bit bored. 
* I won't spoil any specifics but I will say the ending of the game is...not good, in my opinion. 

Pros:

* UI is clean and easy to use. The applications work smoothly without any issues. 
* Gameplay is straight forward and easy to understand. 
* Solid voice acting. 
* Storytelling is pretty engaging. 
* Game very stable, zero crashes or bugs / glitches. 
* No additional DRM beyond Steam.
* No Epic Online Services.

I got the game on sale and puzzle games aren't usually my thing but I wanted to give it a try as it sounded interesting and I like to support indie developers when I can, but this is a game that, despite some story aspects being well-done, the ending soured things for me as well as the bomb defusal mission to the point that I really would not recommend the game to others.

Okay, while I said I liked this game, [b]I think in terms of recommendation, this is more a "maybe" than an outright "yes."[/b] There are several things to consider before you purchase this one, and while I ultimately think you'll enjoy the experience either way, you may be slightly frustrated by at least one or two of these points. I know I was. 

(-) First, the game is short. It took me less than 4 hours to finish it, and that's with several long cut scenes. Speaking of those cut scenes... pay attention to them. I didn't, because some of them seemed pointless, and that led me to the only time I felt truly stuck in this game LOL.

(+) You play as an operator in the FDI, and the entire gameplay involves sitting in front of your computer, connecting dots, and solving puzzles. I absolutely loved it. It was fresh and interesting, and the feeling of things connecting and unraveling was really fun. I actually wish we had more of it—I would've gladly played more hours of more cases, slowly connecting them to this huge conspiracy. It made me hope that someone would make an entire mystery murder game (as opposed to a conspiracy) as "the guy in the chair," slowly unraveling everything and helping the "heroes" solve the mystery. 

(-/+) For a game that's sitting in front of your computer... the stakes are high and so is the tension. I actually got really anxious at parts, in a way that doesn't really happen with most games because, the way everything is set up, WE are Tenner. So I felt like there was a gun aimed at [i]me[/i] at times, LOL. For me, this was a point in favor of the game, but if you're looking for a more relaxed experience, this may not be it. 

(-/+) The ending. Personally? Not a fan. Oh, I loved the reveal. The minute [i]I[/i] started connecting the dots, my stomach dropped. 10/10 for that. But everything after that?... I will be playing the next game, if there is one, but overall, [spoiler]I am not really the kind of person to enjoy an "everybody died" ending. After all the brilliant puzzle solving, I wanted these characters to have a good ending. I have seen people talk about how this was actually a good ending - how Hal is still thwarting the organization 30 years later, and that's realistic and optimistic but damn. I got attached to [i]these[/i] characters. I wanted to see them happy, even if we fail to totally crush the bad guys in the end of the game. And I wanted to understand what the goal of the "bad guys" in this game is, and I don't. They're evil people, but... why are they doing what they're doing? No clue. Which is another thing I don't like. For me, a game needs to be able to stand on its own, even if it's part of a larger narrative. [/spoiler] Essentially, this felt like a game meant to [i]set up[/i] another game, and truthfully, I don't like that.

The only thing this kind of game has to do right is to have a compelling story with a mystery that's satisfying to solve, and The Operator fails on that count. I was expecting something like Papers, Please or The Roottrees are Dead but as a murder mystery, but the only part of the mystery that is solved by the end feels more like a side story to the real mystery, which is never solved at all. The plot twists and character developments make little to no sense and seem like the developers first came up with some "cool" moments, which they struggled (unsuccessfully) to tie together.

I will say there ARE some cool moments - there is a [spoiler]bomb defusal scene[/spoiler] which plays out like [spoiler]a singleplayer version of Keep Talking and Nobody Explodes[/spoiler]; I played it with my girlfriend, with her taking notes while I scoured the supplied in-game manual, and it was very hectic and tense and fun. But as with most plot beats in this game, the circumstances that led to that scene made no sense to us and ultimately the outcome didn't seem to change anything important. Despite being such a short game, it doesn't really seem to branch much based on your actions. The Operator doesn't even have multiple endings, and the one ending it does have is both bleak, unsatisfying, and nonsensical.

Combine this with the fact that - in the style of Papers, Please - there is a lot of information at your disposal throughout the game, but the majority of it is never used (such as the fact that every character bio has a set of fingerprints, but they never come up at all) and I'm left with the impression that the developers had much greater plans but just ran out of time/money and decided to release what they had and call it a day.
