Conspiratorial thinking is kinda like anime girls. Like, okay. So there's this super hot princess from planet catgirl who's on the run from the space mafia, and she just so happens to teleport naked right into your bathtub. While you're in it. And because of this, she's super into you for some reason. Yeah, sounds nice, but this is so insanely removed from how actual relationships form, it's like watching aliens mate (I mean... she is an alien, so...)

And with conspiracies it's like: okay, so there's this ultra-powerful cabal of politicians, billionaires and celebrities, who completely control the society without being spotted... but then they reveal themselves by using symbols in plain sight. And the person to stop them? A bumbling born-into-wealth TV-star who in fact is a 5D-chess player, so all his obvious mistakes are actually genius moves that you just don't get. I don't know guys, seems very legit, but there are a few pieces of this story that make me question its validity.

Think about how a real conspiracy of this scale would work. Incomprehensible wealth would be poured into world-class assassins and operatives to ensure compliance or silence. Evidence would be erased with brutal efficiency, with red herrings and multiple layers of scapegoats; but even then, people are people, and eventually something could possibly slip the cracks. 

The Operator explores this more realistic portrayal of conspiracies, with the scale also being somewhat more realistic. You don't know who you can trust and who you can't. But not everyone (except you) is in on it.

Right?

But hold on. Before you start yelling LOOMINARTY CONFIRMED and smoking dat 420 MLG style, some actual work needs to be done. You're an [strike]FBI[/strike] FDI operator with an access to a pretty sweet database, but also a job to do - to support agents in the field. Whatever confirming of loominarty you'll be doing will have to be squeezed in between protecting and serving those who [strike]are supposed to[/strike] protect and serve. Or perhaps these things could be related?

Wouldn't that be convenient.

Even with all your state-of-the-art tech you'll still have to think outside the box here. And pay attention. You might not find the all-seeing eye, but a funny detail here, a reappearing pattern there, and you just might find something that you're not supposed to.

But it's a dangerous game. For you, and for whoever [i]they[/i] might see as your ally. Things might get tense. Your palms will sweat, your heart will go a little bit faster. Someone's life might be on the line. And you're the only one that picked up the phone.

Still: this little journey might have what you could call flaws. I won't tell you what they are, because I think they don't really alter the value of the experience. You're a clever person; I'm sure you can see what I mean.

(if you're not that clever, you might want to skip this one, I've seen some really funny comments on the forums from people getting stuck because they missed some stuff)

And if my words alone don't convince you, you might want to know that the (achievement-sourced) percentage of people who have beaten the game is 67%. The only game with a number higher than this is Linelith, but that's a puzzle game that can be beaten in an hour. Draw your own conclusions.

Some interesting concepts and a fun story. Cool twist too. Most of the puzzles were relatively straightforward, but the "manual reading" one was actually pretty exciting and interesting, and the "identifying the feed" one was clever. I just could not get past the ridiculous anachronisms popping up constantly, and some very confusing internal logic.

This game takes place in 1992. Everybody has a cell phone, digital photography is commonly accessible, "zoom, enhance" is an actual mechanic. The game's FBI analogue has a database with facial recognition data of nearly everyone in the country? In 1992??? In 2025 sure, but not in 1992. Agents are constantly uploading files to your computer from their phone. At one point, confusingly, an agent apparently sends you physical floppy disks.... via his phone...? Baffling honestly. I was willing to set aside the fact that VoIP didn't exist in 1992 either, but after a while you simply cannot suspend your disbelief any further. 

HAL's "hacking" capabilities are completely inconsistent, and the justifications for why they can't hack a particular thing make no narrative sense a lot of the time. Credit where credit's due though, nothing stands out to me as anachronistic about HAL's methods at least.

There's a big narrative-UX disconnect as well. Initially I thought the "phone calls" you receive from agents are just game objects showing transcripts of audio conversations, but at one point you're instructed to *enter a code into the chat box* as though it were a terminal. So now I'm asked to believe that my computer has been *actually transcribing* phone calls automatically while people are speaking to me, and that I can use this function as a terminal. Completely ridiculous. 

This game would have made way more sense if it were set in the current year, with minimal changes to the story or mechanics, but I think the devs were just too enamoured with the retro aesthetic to let it go so they set it in the 90s anyways. 

Side note: I had annoying bug where my keybinds weren't showing up in-game, so anything where I was required to press a key just had [???] instead. Not game breaking, just annoying.

I really like the genre of mystery games but The Operator felt like it fell short in a few categories for me to recommend this as is. I think they tried to do some interesting things, but I found the story to be a little too 'on rails' for me, and a little too short for the price point. 

One way I'd describe TO is to imagine the intro to a story where you're shown a vast map of the world with a story about it's history and maybe even a quick introduction to the strange artifact you'll be using to navigate the world... And then to only interact with 3% of the map, and to gloss over the history, and the artifact is just a paperweight that we'll never use more than once. That's fine but it does feel like someone went through a lot of trouble to flesh out this world only for it to shrink down to a tiny slice of what they'd made. 

Personally, I'm also not a huge fan of the story. I think they tried to go in a series of different directions at the same time (are you going to play it by the straight and narrow? Are you going to go rogue?) and it all led to the same one place so none of your choices really mattered. The big reveal hinges on you believing that the game's limitations are intentional and not a contrivance of some grand design, so the payout for their big reveals never really felt as good as they could've been. 

So... yeah? I think the story's a little weak/ watered down, but it lives in a frame that I could see the developer building into a bigger/ broader story that would be fun to play. The bones are here for something that could be a cool mystery game, but I'd sooner recommend 'The Roottrees are dead' if you're looking for a better/ more rewarding mystery to sink your time into.

Cons:
* This is really more an interactive novel with some puzzle elements than a game. In addition to its short play time, your choices have little to no impact, it really doesn't matter what you choose in many conversations.

To the question of whether I'd recommend this game: it depends, but probably not. 

Full disclosure up-front: I knew nothing about this game, nor had I done any investigating as to what the game was ultimately meant to be, so my reactions here are likely influenced by it not being quite what I expected or really wanted. 

The Operator is a ultimately a fairly short, story-based narrative dressed in the clothing of a detective game, rather than a detective game where you work through puzzles and solve mysteries. 

The game's mechanics and design were an interesting approach to storytelling, but felt quite underused, which probably goes more to my expectations of wanting a detective puzzle game with a greater variety in cases to solve. In most instances a new mechanic was introduced for one section, only for it to never be used again. 

The story itself is passable. I've consumed my fair share of content in the thriller, detective, mystery and conspiracy genres, and nothing here felt fresh to me in terms of the plot; you could see where the story was going from a mile away and the ultimate outcomes fairly early on. 

If you want a mystery story with conspiracy elements woven in, then this is probably worth a go. If that's not what you're in the market for, then you can probably give this a miss.

I don't think this game is quite what I expected. It's a style of game I'd love to see more of. But while I still mostly enjoyed my time with it, I'm left wanting more.

The story itself is interesting and has enough of those classic thriller movie twist and turns to keep you engaged throughout. Role-playing the "man in the chair" is pretty fun, and you have a few moments that deliver on that promise, at least from a narrative standpoint.

After playing this through once, you'd think the game had multiple endings. You are left wondering if maybe there's some way to correct your mistakes and change the outcome. That is not the case. The ending is pretty bleak, comes pretty quickly (the game itself only being a few hours long at most), and doesn't bring the story to a proper close. I can do without a "good ending", but there's a disappointing lack of closure here.

Broadly speaking, The Operator fails to deliver on the use of "detective skills" it says you'll need in the game's description. You definitely interact with a computer and run a few faux-terminal commands, but most of the time you're just finding a name or a face by clicking the a button that Zoom-Enhances a video CSI style. It sure looks like you're doing the work, but none of it is very challenging and it all feels a little superficial.

There's maybe one section that raises the difficulty and that's because it puts you on a timer and forces you to read an instruction manual. It's the first and only challenging moment the game offers. It was actually a pretty good moment, and the game could have done with a few more scenes this.

I'd not recommend this game to fans of puzzle games who are looking for a challenge, but it's still a fun journey if you want to spend a few hours in the world of a thriller movie. Just don't expect a satisfying ending.

This game has so much going on that I would ideally like to praise but a lot of those same things are also why I didn't really enjoy it.  On the bright side it has a very clever user interface system I like where most of the game is controlled via a "computer", the puzzles range from really easy to more complicated, and the story has some creativity going on.  It's definitely somewhat interesting, very dialogue heavy, and I would not recommend if you're not a strong reader, lover of puzzle games, or if you like a lot of scenery or environment changes.

With that said, the user interface becomes tiring to interact with very quickly.  It's hard to convey a sense of importance or immediate action when most of the puzzles really come down to clicking and having a computer "analyze" random clues.  The puzzles don't scale well in difficulty nor do they feel like they have a good payoff - any skill you learn will either be used again and again because we have to have some way to drive the game or it's a one time use - why did we bother to spend so much time reworking the wheel for no reason? (Example slight spoiler: you will never need to analyze anything other than the one sample in the game).  The instructions are lacking a lot - they have a help button that is definitely useful but there's an element of figure it out here that at times seems un-necessary.  I really don't understand not sticking to more tried and true puzzle formats particularly because they would have felt more rewarding, helped the game, and surely been easier to execute with more precision.

As an avid fan of narrative-driven puzzle games, I recently delved into "The Operator," developed by Bureau 81. Released on July 22, 2024, this game offers a unique experience by placing players in the role of Evan Tanner, an operator at the fictional Federal Defence Intelligence agency. Your primary task is to assist field agents by analysing evidence and providing real-time support, all from behind a computer screen.

The game's immersive design truly makes you feel like a part of a larger investigative team. The puzzles are well-crafted, requiring keen attention to detail without becoming overly frustrating. Each case you handle reveals a piece of a larger conspiracy, keeping your curiosity piqued from start to finish. The narrative is compelling, reminiscent of classic detective stories, and unfolds at a pace that keeps you engaged throughout the approximately five-hour gameplay. 


However, the game isn't without its flaws. Some plot twists are predictable, and the voice acting can be hit-or-miss at times. Additionally, while the main storyline is captivating, I found myself wishing for more side cases to further explore the game's mechanics and world. 


In conclusion, "The Operator" is a commendable addition to the narrative puzzle genre. It offers an immersive and engaging experience that is well worth your time, especially if you're a fan of detective stories and investigative gameplay. Despite its minor shortcomings, it stands out as a solid and enjoyable game.

The game really was not what I expected. From the store page, I thought it would be fairly puzzle focused, with a lot of scanning evidence and connecting dots. But in reality, it plays out more like a visual novel with some very simple puzzles thrown in. There were multiple elements that seemed like they would be recurring features, but were used a single time and never again. Many pieces of evidence are teased, but are never actually shown before the game ends. The game feels like it ends *way* too quickly. It took me just over three hours to finish. I'm fine with shorter games, but there's so much potential here that goes nowhere because the game ends so soon.

On the plus side, the presentation is great. Despite mostly being a computer screen, the visuals have a certain flare to them that leans into the setting. The soundtrack compliments the narrative at every step, swelling at big reveals and calming down after tense moments. And the voice actors give solid performances. No complaints on this aspect.

As for the narrative, it's fairly compelling. You can definitely see a lot of the twists coming before they happen, but the presentation makes it interesting to see play out regardless. That being said, it again suffers from being too short. You're meant to be unraveling a big conspiracy over the course of the game, but by the time it's over, it feels like you've barely stuck your toes in. I was invested in what was happening, had just had a big reveal, and then... suddenly the credits are rolling.

There are definitely things to like about this game, but I have a hard time recommending it, especially if your mostly here for that "Investigation" tag. It's too short, too easy, and doesn't quite live up to what it says on the box. It feels like a demo for a larger game, but I kind of just wanted the larger game to begin with.

I recommend it ... but with some qualifications. 

So, the presentation is excellent. Really builds a strong atmosphere of mystery. There are points when you really feel like you're an operator for a field agent uncovering a major conspiracy. The game does a very good job of doing that. Some of the puzzles took some thinking. They're not super-difficult, but they all make sense in the context of the game and there's not a lot of handholding. Overall, I like how it's all presented.

However ... what I didn't realize is that this is more visual novel than a true puzzle game. It's not a pure visual novel - there is some genuine gameplay here. And that gameplay is pretty good. But ultimately, the gameplay is to trigger the next scene. You can't really "fail" - or at least, you can't fail in a way that will affect the story.

I had believed the game to be a puzzler in the vein of Obra Dinn or Orwell. And I would say the gameplay is as good in part. But after a while, I could "see the rails" - see that at its core, it's a visual novel.

However, that's not why I was disappointed.

The bigger problem I had with the game is that I felt it was ... too short. Not in terms of game length - but in terms of the plot. It felt like it ended right when the plot was getting interesting. 

Putting spoilers on anything further:
[spoiler]Where the game ends, when the intrigue is getting intense and the identity twist is revealed ... I felt almost like that's where the real story is starting. 

Up until this point, our protagonist has just been faceless tech guy who doesn't have a role in the story - and suddenly now we understand how he ties into the conspiracy. And we also understand just what kind of terrible enemy we're up against. 

With this dramatic twist, we now understand the protagonist and his role in the story - as well as true nature and threat of the antagonist that he faces. The stakes have been made clear. The die is cast, the point of no return is reached. 

The question is, what happens now? What does our protagonist do with his new forbidden knowledge? And how can he defeat this terrible enemy?... but instead - the story unceremoniously ends right there. Not only is it kind of a bummer of an ending - but it feels like you stopped telling me this story exactly at the point where it became interesting. Right at the point where things had fully shifted from "Government Bureau Employee Simulator" to "Global Spy Conspiracy Thriller". Our agency has revealed they're evil and they betrayed us, we're gonna go rogue, and take the conspiracy down .... no, wait, actually, that's the end. [/spoiler] 
 
[spoiler]It'd be like if moments after Jason Bourne realized that he was a secret agent and that assassins were trying to kill him ... he just died and the movie ended.

Or, to use a videogame equivalent - it'd be like if right when it's revealed that Doki Doki Literature Club is not actually an anime dating sim ... the game just ended.

There's no resolution. The story feels incomplete. If anything, this feels like it should be the prologue to the real plot. Like a teaser that gives us a glimpse of "OMG these guys are really bad". 

Actually, at the end, when it shifts to HAL's perspective - I thought that was where the real game was about to begin. like, "Twist, Tanner dies in the prologue! You're actually playing as HAL. How will HAL defeat the Organization?" ... But then the credits rolled.[/spoiler] 
 
[spoiler]Part of the problem was that I figured out the twist long before it was revealed. I wasn't being clever, either - it was clear from the opening cutscene that we were not playing as some anonymous rando. We are obviously someone who is involved with this conspiracy in some way. As events played out, the only possibilities were either (a) you were secretly one of the missing people or (b) you were secretly the Ghost. When it became clear you weren't the Ghost ... well, there's only one missing person who we know by name, so that must be you.[/spoiler] 
 
I will say I was thoroughly engaged up until the ending. Even when it started to become clear that the story was more on rails that I'd hoped - I didn't mind because the presentation was so good and the story had me hooked. 

But when it ended ... I felt very disappointed because I was like, "Wait, we're ending it here? That's it?"

So I guess that's my recommend. It's a very well-done experience and the devs clearly were doing something right to keep me gripped. I intended to just try the game for a bit and ended up finishing it in one setting. But it really surprised me that it ended where it did.

This is an excellent, short puzzle and story game as an Operator in the FDI assisting agents with cases

The game opens with a cut scene which you watch and this sets the tone. Then you see a computer terminal boot up and you log in. This is the start of your job as an operator for the FDI (Federal Department of Intelligence). This is the main screen you see and involves taking calls, running through evidence and assisting agents with their cases.

There is a small cast of characters – you assist a few agents, you hear from the director, who is a friend, and you have a direct supervisor. There are also a couple of other people you hear from. To start with the calls walk you through the basics of the set up and the mechanics you will be using. Then you are given your first call from an agent.

The element of “assisting” agents is fun and about solving puzzles. Finding people in databases, working out how to get evidence from clues in video and audio files and some careful reading of instructions and asking questions. I found the puzzles varied, fun, hard (but not too hard) and appropriate to the setting. The difficulty curve generally increases as the game progresses.

The other people are interesting and I generally liked them, particularly the agents. They were varied, plausible and interesting. There were a couple of dialogue choices where I would have not chosen from the options given, but mostly they were plausible too.

The progression of the different cases builds the stories, tone and difficulty of the puzzles. Also, the puzzles generally get harder, although one or two of the later ones are still quite quick. 

Video and audio are basic but effective, this isn't a high budget game but makes excellent use of what it has.

Saving happens when you exit the game, this isn't particularly clear to start with. I think the rule is that if you are between cases then you just save, but if you are in the middle of a call, then it will take you back to the start of the call/case. Which has the advantage of letting you return to the game and not be in the middle of something complicated, it is also something you can use if you want another attempt at a puzzle (as you can fail some of them).

I won't say too much about the ending. There is only one ending (confirmed by the game designer) and it does seem a little sequel-hook like. Also, there is a post credits scene.

In general, this is a really interesting puzzle story game and be aware of it's comparatively short length.

This review is unfortunate, because as much as I'd like to recommend the game, there's a few gripes I have with it.

First and foremost, I want to stress, this game is great and has a good hook for its plot. The mechanics it employs are varied and fun, and you do get to feel like an FBI agent working on cases alongside others. The game does a lot to nail the feel and vibe, the UI is also great and intuitive. The game's main issue isn't one singular thing, rather, it's a collection of small, minor nitpicks that ultimately end up souring the entire experience. Without trying to spoil anything, I'm going to try and summarise my complaints. 

First and foremost, the ending left me wanting. If there was an alternate ending you could achieve by using information you've gathered, it'd be one thing, but you don't get to do anything and then it just sort of ends abruptly, teasing a sequel or DLC. This is the very definition of a cliffhanger, and as such, extremely unsatisfying.

This could have been remedied if the game length was longer. But the game's barely clocking in 3 hours, you could probably beat it in 2. And, likely because of said short runtime, the game features a very small cast of characters. This unfortunately results in a somewhat predictable list of potential suspects, lessening any impacts felt from reveals that you likely saw coming.

Perhaps my biggest disappointment with how short the game was, is that the actual mechanics were unique and interesting! The puzzles were good and it introduced so many systems, one time you're analyzing chemical compounds based on formulas, another time you're disarming a bomb while given a huge manual of possibilities. And each of these varied activities happens exactly once. You spend all that time learning, understanding and mastering a skill only for it to literally not be relevant again.

This all could have perhaps been remedied by a sort of "endless mode" that generates cases and solutions, but that does not exist. And likely never will, because the game is far more focused on "immersion" as a central mechanic than gameplay. You spend a good solid 20 minutes of said 3 hours being forced to watch "immersive" unskippable cutscenes that did not need to last as long as they did. I say "immersive", because they use minimalism and only show you blurry, obfuscated imagery, which is kind of neat and saves on budget, but also means you don't even get eye candy.

Ultimately, this feels like a passion project with the wrong focus, which is a shame, because what it does right, it excels at. It's difficult to recommend this when there's games such as Cyber Manhunt 1 & 2 out that cost less and are far, far more superior in terms of value and vision. The devs are talented, and I will keep a close eye on any of their future projects, but if "The Operator 2" doesn't provide something substantially more... substantial, I can't see myself recommending that either.

TL;DR
Overall a solid, if short, experience. If you like games similar to Killer Frequency, Hypnospace Outlaw, or even Papers Please, you will enjoy this. I felt the story was paced well enough and presented well enough to keep my interest to the end. My only complaints are the length of the game, a lack of content, and I had the story fairly well figured out before the climax. The puzzles were well put together, for the most part, but none of them felt difficult and I completed them pretty quickly, and enjoyed doing so. For 15$ I think it's worth your time if you're looking for a few hours to kill doing detective work. On sale I definitely recommend it.

GAMEPLAY:
The gameplay is pretty simplistic. As stated above similar to the likes of Hypnospace Outlaw where you navigate a computer system using different apps and given information (files) to solve puzzles. The puzzles themselves I felt weren't overly difficult, but done well enough to definitely have me pay more attention to various things. They also do a great job with handling a few very important plot points in the game. One section, in particular, did get me rather anxious. Overall it does its job well, and I enjoyed pretty much all of it. The only problem I had overall with gameplay was the lack of content. It gives you some interesting tools to utilize, then just sort of forgets about them.

SOUND:
I really enjoyed what they did with this game. The music really fit the moments and added some flair to various points in the game. The ambient sound and environmental sounds are also done VERY well to play parts in the game. It may not blow your mind, but I appreciate the amount of effort they put forth in this front. The soundtrack is quite good.

STORY:
They do a good job giving a good detective story to play out. You may or may not figure out the twists and turns it will take. Unfortunately I had some of the big reveals pegged within the first hour. On the other hand, I still enjoyed it enough to keep going. It won't blow your mind or take you into the depths of the universe they created; it gives you what it needs to, and executes it well. I don't care if a story blows my mind, so long as I have fun experiencing it, which I did here.

As a side note for the story, they did do a great job with a few moments of making them actually very tense. My only complaint, as stated above, is that it felt too short.


IN CONCLUSION:
The Operator is a solid entry into this detective-like puzzle-solving Operating System-simulator genre. I enjoyed my time with it, I do enjoy the mechanics of utilizing a computer in game to solve various puzzles with information that is available, but you have to search for. While sort, it didn't overstay its welcome and accomplished what it set out to do. I will greatly look forward to another game of this style if they decide to do one!

The plot is above average, the graphics are pretty solid, and the audio is well suited.

There are some teething pains, such as unskippable blurs that count as cutscenes and if you ever replay a section you'll be sitting through the exact same dialogue all over again. There's also some issues with clickable areas in some scenes and a certain technical scene being a little hard to parse, since the manual uses terminology that doesn't *quite* fit.

However, the experience was quite lovely. The technical implementation is far above average, with dynamic windows, active text scrolling, and audio cues when you scroll to a certain section of text. It's extremely well coded. I see a lot of Unity games with UI issues, but this was as solid an implementation as I've seen. Well thought out, well executed, marvelous job!

And the amount of effort for a single dev, even with the support provided, is astonishing. Making this in *only* three years is quite impressive.

I do wish it was a more dynamic experience, but that requires an astonishing amount of work. As a stepping stone to future work, this is quite excellent. I'm happy to see this particular genre of game get more entires of this quality, and I'll be keeping an eye on this developer.

Highly recommended.

Other games in this genre would have made it a permanent element of the game moving forward, integrating it alongside other tools and resources to solve cases. In sum, this is a great demo for a game that came out in 2013, but better, more complete, more elaborate, more creative games already exist that do the same things.

review:
I love cyber sleuthing games with my favorites being Orwell, Cyber Manhunt, and Her Story. So this definitely scratched an itch for me. 

Story: Story is pretty straightforward with an overarching conspiracy you have to unravel. Honestly, its not groundbreaking but it keeps you invested. What elevates it for me is the music kicking in at certain moments to heighten tension. The soundtrack for this game is not bad. 

Forewarned the story is short with most of the negative reviews highlighting that. While I wouldve liked to have had more, I will say that I prefer games being straight to the point rather than needless filler. You can get maybe 3 hours out of this so if that is not worth 14 dollars for you, then maybe skip this.  

Gameplay: Its a typical point and click adventure using an enhanced 90s style computer interface. Aside from the usual info gathering, the puzzles are thoroughly challenging with my favorite being a bomb defusal segment that I found to be quite challenging. But in a fun way. I wouldve liked to use the tools more like the bomb defusal and chemical analyzer more than once. It wouldve added another layer of challenge to the game.


I would definitely recommend buying and experiencing this game whether it be on sale or not.

If you think this is a game where you analyze crimes while searching for increasingly complicated data you are wrong.
If you think this is a narrative game with multiple branches and endings depending on your decisions you are wrong.

Its just a linear visual novel... and was sold to me as something different.

I almost never leave reviews, so bear with me.

I was kind of enthralled by the demo: I loved the idea of drawing connections, of looking something up in one database and comparing it to the next database and finding it on a list retrieved earlier.  Then...well, I'm [i]not[/i] going to say is "bait and switch"; I think the demo is a fair representation of the game.  But the game did go in different directions than I'd hoped: for instance, the connection-drawing is in many ways the core of the game, but there was a lot of stuff around it: dialogue choices, minigames  ("oh, look, mastermind"), occasional long cutscenes.

At its core the game is a thriller, which is not really my genre.  (There's literally a "Them", which I think is the same as "The Organization", which is what you get if you ask LLMs to summarize the thriller genre.)  I could have guessed that, probably, but there's so much that seems to pay homage to [i]The X-Files[/i] (the FBI in the 1990s, the typewritten location captions, your boss is literally named Skinner for heaven's sake), and one of the first cases you get is alien-abduction-based.  This ended up being way more "thriller" in tone than X-Files was.

But to be clear: I didn't hate it!  I wish Steam had a scale more subtle than "yes/no", because I want to give it a "qualified yes" or maybe a "no, but if it's your thing, then yes".  There's a lot to like here: the atmosphere (even if you could practically see the words "cue dramatic music" at major plot twists), the interface, even a lot of the writing and plot.  Much of the voice acting is good; I really liked Pendell and Walker; Andrews less so.  (The two coroner reports, even less.)  And the [spoiler]bomb-defusing scene[/spoiler] did a great job with the tone.

Premise Overview:
You, Evan Tanner, are hired as as part of the Operator Program in which you work to support field agents of the fictional FDI in solving their crimes. Except, there's a bigger evil at play than your regular homicide perpetrator or arson case.


For people who love desktop style games (such as Her Story and Telling Lies) this is a goldmine. A mixture of puzzle solving, enigmatic storytelling with a capturing atmosphere, frankly fantastic voice acting and investing gameplay, The Operator strives to keep you engaged in the progression of the main, if too short, main plot line.

While the twist is admittedly a little predictable, this is a game you can enjoy none-the-less that keeps you on edge with effective sound (such as a fantastic musical score and effects such as reverberated and slow footsteps during tense moments). It fits perfectly into the hearts of those who enjoy these types of games - such as myself.

I just wish there was more in there aside from the main story. All the cases you receive are connected, which makes sense but takes away from the realistic sense the game does actually have, and you receive a whole wanted list of criminals - of which only one appears. I would have loved a side story about one of the criminals on there who was the leader of a cult.

Now, the ending. It's cold and it slaps you in the face, quite frankly. You go through all this, discover everything Evan's been through just for it to be a swift chop and done and that just doesn't seem fair and it's a little bit of a let down to have it happen so quick.  Though, there is potential and lead for a sequel.

Regardless, I really do recommend this game. I wish it was longer and I wish there was more too it but that just encourages me to keep an eye on the developers and snap up anything else they come out with.

The Operator is an incredibly immersive first-person game where you step into the shoes of an FDI operator, guiding field agents through tense, high-stakes situations. The game hooks you with its realistic atmosphere, detailed calls, and the way it makes you feel like a vital part of every operation.

At first, you're focused on supporting agents in their day-to-day missions, but as the game progresses, strange and unsettling elements start creeping into your calls. What begins as routine work grows into a gripping, larger-than-life case that pulls you in emotionally and mentally. The story escalates masterfully, and the twists near the end are nothing short of mind-blowing.

While the gameplay is phenomenal, the only downside is its brevity. The main story can be completed in about 3-4 hours, and there isn’t much replay value since the narrative is linear. Personally, I adore this game, but I really wish it had an endless mode with randomized calls or some kind of story expansion to dive deeper into the experience.

That said, The Operator delivers a thrilling, unforgettable ride. For what it is, it’s a masterpiece—and I wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone looking for a unique and engaging game. Here's hoping the developers expand on this concept in the future!

This game is top notch. As an old school adventure fan this felt like a true Rise of the Dragon, Jeff Tunnell style game which has been sorely lacking in the current market. What I mean by that specifically is that the post-Life is Strange adventure genre has had a long period of hammy, melodramatic social messaging meant to impress small cliques of games journalists for accolades in their astroturfed outlets. The REAL culprit was ABUSE! Or HOMOPHOBIA! Or RACISM! And the game was a METAPHOR! This plot device was not terribly interesting to begin with but due to the applause and funding that comes to such projects, it left us with a decade of such tripe as developers scratched and clawed to be next in line at the Attaboy Club, with each new offering being more hamfisted and alarmist than the last (check my review of 'Jessika' for a hilarious instance of this).

The Operator, however, is just a good old fashioned hard boiled story about cover ups and corruption.  It has a couple of flaws, the primary one being the blurred out bokeh filters meant to act as cutscenes. There is a sorta-kinda in-story explanation for this, and a reason for it to justify a later puzzle, but really it just comes across as a way to avoid paying for cutscenes and as a way to bridge days together, which is understandable enough for a small team with not a lot of money. In future, I'd recommend bridging the days with some kind of interactive option at the character's apartment or neighborhood, or by just using comic book style art for the cutscenes. In any case that complaint is a nothing burger, the game is well worth it and I look forward to more!

Tl;Dr: The Operator is an absolute gem and probably one of my favorite gaming experiences this year. It nails its atmosphere and story, with a few small quirks holding it back from perfection.

[h1] What I Loved [/h1]
[h3]The Layout:[/h3] The environments and flow are super well-designed. You’re never lost, but there’s enough to explore to keep things interesting.

[h3]Subtle 90s Vibes:[/h3] The aesthetic is on point—just the right touch of nostalgia without feeling overdone. If you love that slightly grainy, retro tech vibe, you’ll be right at home.

[h3]UI:[/h3] Clean, simple, and fits the tone perfectly. You never feel like you’re fighting the menus, which is always a win.

[h3]Voice Acting:[/h3] Honestly, top-tier. The performances are so natural, and they add so much depth to the story.
Pacing: The game knows when to keep things moving and when to let moments breathe. It’s a tight, well-paced experience.

[h3]The Ending:[/h3] I won’t spoil anything, but wow—it sticks the landing. One of those endings that makes you sit there for a second and just think, wish for more but grow more satisfied with what (little) you know.

[h1]What I Didn’t Love[/h1]

[h3]No Narrative Skip:[/h3] This is a big one for achievement hunters. If you miss something, you’ll have to sit through all the dialogue again, which can get frustrating.

[h3]No Replay Value:[/h3] They’re upfront about this, but I still think it’s a shame. The world and story are so good that even small additions—alternate choices or alternating riddles ([spoiler]Read: Bomb[/spoiler]) or hidden paths—would’ve added a lot.

[h1]Final Thoughts[/h1]
If you’re into story-driven games with a great atmosphere, The Operator is 100% worth your time. It’s short, sweet, and delivers an experience that sticks with you. Sure, it’s a one-and-done kind of deal, but honestly, it’s so good while it lasts that I didn’t mind too much.

A very interesting idea. I picked this up after having played the Home Safety Hotline game. I feel this genre of Computer Screen based narrative is an up and coming format for storytelling that has a lot of potential. 

In the case of The Operator, we see a well thought out concept of an intelligence bureau, agents who need help in the field and yourself as the operator tasked with helping them correlate information remotely. Quickly the game establishes the breadcrumbs of an overarching mystery that slowly unravels over the course of your investigation.

I found the narrative to be quite gripping from the start and the gameplay to be endearing, the use of the computer screen and phone conversations feels very personal and the side characters you encounter are given enough personality to be endearing as you assist their investigations.

I'd say if this is your type of game then it is 100% worth a go. And for such a reasonable price I'd say give it a chance if you are on the fence.

I will be eagerly awaiting any possible follow up to this story and world.

Overall, I adored this game.  I struggle with this next phrase because i don't fully mean it and understand why it is the way it is... but I'm glad I bought it on sale and not full price as it's not quite worth the full price.  I mostly say this due to game length and lack of choice in endings.  I took a look and it looks like this might be a first time game from this dev, who I'm guessing is solo or very small which is VERY exciting to see if this is their freshman showing.

Things I LOVED:
-Dynamic story telling.  There was a clear storyline running through from start to finish.  Not overly convoluted, not too cliche or simple.  Were the twists a little predictable?  Maybe a few.  But that didn't take away from the impact when they hit anyway.  The pacing of those drops were excellently done.
-Style was lovely.  I REALLY dug the overall look of the game.  The various tools you got to us, the puzzles you go to solve... all from a single terminal.  It made me think of a hacking game from the early 00s of gaming sites that I loved to play over and over.
-The voice acting was excellent.  Really stellar work.
-The game itself.  It's just really enjoyable.  It was well paced, the mystery was fun, the story was easy to follow, the puzzles were a bit easy but a few had some real challenges in there.  One puzzle was a bit too much of a lateral thinking puzzle, BUT that was one of the best twists of the whole game so I can overlook it. 

Things I wish were different (not bad, just things I wanted more of):
-it's far too short.  It took me about 4 hours to complete and that was going very slow and taking my time, looking at my phone a lot and doing a few other things at the same time. (thanks ADHD)  The story telling and plot that the game is driving could easily have been a full scale game.  And I'd pay good money for it, too.  This is top notch story telling from a new dev and I hope we see more.
-Lack of use of cool tools.  You're introduced to several cool mini puzzles throughout the game like a car analyzer, a bomb diffuser, and chemical component analyzer.  All of them have robust rules and options with them.  And they're all used only once.  You gave us so many cool toys.. let us play with them!!
-No story diversity with a [spoiler] really weak and bad ending [/spoiler].  While the story they have given is lovely, your choices don't matter.  There is just that ending.  I wanted more options, i wanted to affect the story with how i played and wanted the game reward cleverness (i.e. if you found a certain name on a certain list before you were told to.)

All that being said, if you like mystery games, if you like hack style games, this is a great choice.  I am very excited to see what this dev does in the future.  If this is their first showing, we are in for some real gems in the future!!

I want to give this an honest review, because although I enjoyed it and the game does have a lot of potential, there are some setbacks to it as well.

Positives:
-The gameplay is fun and paced well. It never felt boring or slow, and the storyline was intriguing and kept me interested throughout.
-The detective work was interesting, but not too challenging. Other than [spoiler] the bomb defusing puzzle which was super annoying and convoluted out of nowhere and with a time limit that made it even worse [/spoiler] I could progress easily without feeling like it was too simple.
-The game's ui was easy to use and had nice to look at.

Negatives:
-It's well written, but really short. As you can tell from my playtime, it moved super quickly. While the story was still satisfying for the most part, it felt like it ended prematurely due to the short length. I would have liked to have seen at least a few more days worth of gameplay.
-The ending felt, to me, very unsatisfying. [spoiler] Although I'm sure, given the after credits scene, this is meant to be a cliff hanger for the next game, the way it ended just left me feeling like all the work I had done was meaningless and therefore the game had been meaningless. That's not to say the ending was all bad or should be completely changed. But, for example, if it had ended with one person being apprehended, or something similar to give some sense of conclusion, it would have been a lot better. As it is, I finished it somewhat annoyed. As if I had wasted all that effort for no reward, and an unfinished storyline. [/spoiler] This criticism is somewhat of a personal opinion, I know, but it really soured my view of the game at the end. Which was a shame, because up until that very moment I was super engrossed in the story and really enjoying it.

Overall, I enjoyed the gameplay and story right up until the final minute. So I would recommend the game, if you got it on sale or don't mind that it is very short, and you aren't put off by the thought of an abrupt ending. I think this studio did a great job producing it though and telling a story, and look forward to their next game. I only hope their next ending will feel a bit more satisfying for the player.

The game puts you in the shoes of an FDI operator (ingame version of FBI), helping field operatives behind a computer screen.
There's a huge conspiracy you stumble into, aided by a hacker.
Without going into story spoilers, I saw the "twist" from the very start, obfuscated by a small wrinkle that doesn't actually play into the story at all unfortunately.

The game leaves many loose ends, and ends rather abruptly and is rather short overall (playtime 4,4 h on steam).

After finishing it it was obvious the game was very constrained by budget, and story wise seems the devs bite off more than they could chew or had much bigger plans for it. For that reason, the game kinda ends on a cliff hanger and your "choices" don't really matter, there is only one ending- my bet is that they want to make a sequel if this sells enough copies.
With all that being said, there is some amazing atmosphere, voice acting and tense and well written moments to experience in this. I'd love to see what the devs would be able to cook up given more room/time/money/people to breath and spread their wings.

"The Operator" masterfully weaves storytelling and gameplay, making you feel like a real detective. The attention to detail and realistic scenarios create a captivating atmosphere.

Pros:

- High replayability

- Engaging storyline

Cons: None notable

If you're a fan of investigative games or looking for a unique gaming experience, "The Operator" is a must-play.

Highly Recommended!

I grade The Operator A-. This is an excellent investigation game with a great premise and fantastic presentation, including the music. While it doesn't have Hollywood-style hacking, given that its setting is in 1992 and you're working in a government alphabet agency, the developers nailed the look and feel of a stripped down government UI. Even right down to a part where you use an even [i]older[/i] computer and the visual area changes from 16:9 to 4:3. Nice touch.

The story is very well written. I didn't detect a single typo or weird turn of phrase. A lot of detective games here on Steam are made by non-English developers, and so they tend to get wonky in localization. The Operator does not have that issue. The story is almost entirely logical and internally consistent, and it was fun to experience.

The only thing is the story's wheels fell off at the very end. While the story beats and twists were a bit obvious, the final hard twist -- though it was presented really well -- makes absolutely no logical sense even within the context of the world that is presented to us. I come away from it with a lot more questions, but not the good "What are they going to do next?" kind. It's more the "Why did the basic premise happen in the first place?" kind. Unless there was some subtlety I missed, I can think of a thousand reasons why the first step of the plot shouldn't have happened, and that sort of makes the ending a little bit of a letdown.

But don't let that dissuade you. I'm happy to have bought the game and supported the developer, especially because the gameplay was excellent. I really enjoyed the act of investigating as a government agent and having tools like face-scanning and an omni-database just a mouse click away. Don't get me wrong, I enjoy games with hacking -- whether Hollwood hacking like Orwell or more script-based hacking like HackNet -- but it was really fun to be an agent for the "other side" and just have some improbable tools at my fingertips. If there is a sequel, while I hope the writing makes a little more logical sense, I really encourage the devs to keep the gameplay just as it is.

The Operator is a very short (3 to 4 hours at best) interactive visual novel with good production value. The interface looks clean and easy to use, the voice acting is good, and the interactive elements are pretty decent. For a visual novel. 

It is presented, however, as a game of deduction and puzzle solving. The puzzles and deductions are shallow with too much handholding. As you progress new mechanics are introduced, and then discarded immediately after. This gives the mistaken impression that much more content is waiting for you and puzzles will get more difficult. And then the game is over.

The story is equally shallow. The opening scene reveals too much, making the big reveal at the end something you can piece together within a few minutes of playing the game. The ending is a cliffhanger of sorts, but it makes this game feel like the opening chapter of a larger story that has not been written. Worse is that none of the conspiracy is ever explained, leaving you with many questions that are unlikely to be answered. There are no divergent paths, only one ending, and zero replay value.

If you go into this game expecting a visual novel, you will have an entertaining few hours with an okay story and underwhelming finale. If you go into this game expecting deduction, investigation, and puzzle solving, you will find only disappointment. This ultimately leads to my negative review. For a visual novel it is too short with an unresolved story, and for an investigation game the puzzles are too simple. The Operator has a lot of unmet potential, which is a shame.

I'm only giving this a thumbs down because I believe this is marketed incorrectly. I loved the game for what it is, a visual novel. But this is not necessarily a detective game, and I'd argue not even really investigative.
The game follows one story line, and kind of fools you into thinking your choices matter when they really don't. For example, I attempted every dialogue option to not work with HAL, but that didn't matter, I had to work with them anyway.
The tools used are awesome; facial recognition, Human Database, lab analysis. But we only use some of these things once or a few times at most.
Don't get me wrong, the story is fantastic, and I genuinely loved my time with it. I agree with a lot of the other reviews that this should be way longer, but overall, I think the game is marketed incorrectly which is where I can't recommend it. I, and it seems a lot of others, went into this with the idea I would be solving multiple cases, using the technology multiple times, maybe even an endless mode where there's multiple variations of possible cases. 
I do think it's a great game, the immersion into the FDI computer is fantastic, the art style/graphics are perfect, everything ran smoothly. I mean genuinely top marks across (most of) the board. But it did leave me wanting more, I really dislike that we only used some of the tools once, and my choices didn't matter. All that being said, I absolutely would purchase another game from this dev.

This game only has one ending, and only less than 2½ - 3 hours of content in total, making the cost per played hour very high. 
The one singular ending is quite bad, and even though there are many dialogue options, there are no actual meaningful choices to be made.
There are numerous quite long and somewhat boring unskippable cut scenes. However one could argue that having no skip option is acceptable due to it being somewhat important to pay attention to the them. And since there's only one ending, there's no replayability, and so there's no need to have a skip option. Though realistically, and as others have pointed out, the most probable reason for not having a skip option is to extend the required playtime to over 2 hours so the game cannot be refunded through Steam.
The game has a lot of dialogue, and not a lot of gameplay. What little actual gameplay there is, is enjoyable enough I guess, but also pretty simplistic and easy. This can be seen as both a positive and a negative. If you're looking for any sort of a challenge/puzzle, you will not find it in this game. This game should be definitely thought of as a visual novel more than a puzzle game.
The story itself is mediocre and actually pretty shallow, which is very bad for a game that consists mainly of the story.
The dialogue is fully voice-acted (except for [spoiler]HAL[/spoiler] and the protagonist), which is a definite plus. The voice acting is also pretty high-quality. However I cannot help but feel like way too much developer effort and money was put into the voice acting, when it should've been put into other aspects of the game.
The soundscape and the soundtrack are also good, but really nothing out of the ordinary.

Overall, The Operator is a short, pricey mediocre dialogue-heavy and minimal-gameplay game with high-quality voice acting and heavy hand-holding and railroading, and with only one ending. It feels like the game was designed to be just long enough to make it impossible to refund after reaching the ending (which in fairness one shouldn't do regardless, if they enjoyed the game and reached the ending).

I cannot recommend anything else but to watch someone else such as a YouTuber play this game. I think that will actually add way more to the experience than buying the game and playing it on your own.

Review for The Operator on Steam

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ (5/5)

The Operator is a standout tactical shooter that excels in every aspect. The game combines deep strategy with gripping storytelling, offering a rewarding experience from start to finish. The mission design is superb, the graphics are stunning, and the real-time command system adds layers of tactical depth. The narrative is engaging, with excellent voice acting and a compelling plot that keeps you hooked. With high replay value and ongoing updates, this game is a must-play for fans of the genre. Highly recommended!

First things first - the game needs a sequel! May that serve as a testament to how fun this particular title is. The entire game is you exploring the narrative of the story through the interface of your computer terminal at the FDI, supporting field agents in their investigations. Analysing evidence, using various tools to ascertain information and ultimately being drawn into a conspiracy with quite the twist at the end of it -hence the need for a sequel. If you are looking for a chill, relaxing romp of a story you can't go wrong with this one.

This is definitely one of the games of all time. An experience. Immersive, poignant story with a deep lore for a 3-4 hours playthrough. Music is awesome and fitting. A solid 9/10. Only wish it was longer.

The Operator was so unique and so fun, and genuinely floored me several times. There's a handful of story pieces that maybe I'd do differently, but nothing that would deter me from the game or from recommending it. Puzzles are challenging without feeling impossible, and somehow I felt affection for some of the characters. Wish the POV character was voice acted, but otherwise I absolutely loved this game

What an amazing experience this game is.
A well written story with excellent pacing, and also very good voice acting. It features amazing sound design that really cements the suspense and excitement that this game portrays so well.

The gameplay is simplistic, but shows a lot of thought and care in its design.
You play with a virtual tabletop where you'll navigate files, folders and the chat-system you utilise to communicate with agents. You'll be scanning pictures and videos for details, and cross-check data with the company database that lists any person you can identify with a full name or via face recognition, among other things...

As I finished the game I was filled with a hunger for more. And the systems implemented in this game leaves nigh limitless potential for future projects based on the same concept. I loved every second playing this game, and I hope to see more from this developer in the future.

I feel it is worth mentioning that, one of the more unforgiving elements of this game is that you are unable to save and restart at the beginning of a chapter/day. Therefore, if you miss an achievement, you have to start the game all over again. This brings me to the next unforgiving aspect of this game which is that no dialogue or cut scene is skippable or able to be fast-forwarded (e.g. clicking to make dialogue scroll faster). 

Despite the fact that these elements made the game a little more frustrating, I welcome the challenge. It doesn't take away from my positive review nor my recommendation for others to check this game out. If anything, it makes the achievements feel earned. Additionally, the game is not very long. So, a few restarts shouldn't lock the player into an unrelenting commitment of innumerable hours. I put just 6.5 hours into the game and, to put my point into perspective, I restarted the game twice -- to get all 13 achievements.

GREAT Experience!! Despite its relatively short length, The Operator left me thoroughly engrossed in every minute of gameplay. The intuitive puzzles, combined with the engaging narrative, make it a standout title in the genre. My only complaint is that I was left wanting more by the end of it.

If you’re a fan of narrative-driven games and enjoy solving intricate puzzles, I highly recommend giving “The Operator” a try. It’s a game that tests your detective skills and keeps you on the edge of your seat from start to finish.

If you are looking for a good puzzle/detective guy in the chair game to scratch that itch made by an indie developer to entertain you for 3 hours with great gameplay, great puzzles that don't hold your hand and are satisfying to solve, great voice acting, introducing a couple of interesting game mechanics beyond "click face and search for name here" and a pretty good linear story, then this is the game for you. I bought it at 10% off and really enjoyed it, will definitely be on the look out for the next game this developer makes, and would recommend it to anyone with the expectation that its a good indie game.  

If you are looking for a deep, multi ending detective game where choices matter and there's endless replayability, this is not the game for you. I think the two critiques I see the most of is that fact the game is short and doesn't have multiple endings. For the length side, I think complaining that a game isn't long enough is a pretty good complaint to have. The game isn't perfect, but its entertaining and I hope the developer makes a longer game in the future using the success from this game to better utilize some of the interesting game mechanics that get introduced but then not used again (there's a few). 

Whether it's worth the price is subjective. The developer gave the reasoning that it's about the length of a movie, around the price of similar games, and so that's why it's at the price that it is. I don't know how much that justifies the price for this game, which I feel is a few dollars more expensive than similar games, but since I liked the demo, the movie comparison seemed reasonable enough for me (at least given some reason instead of no reason at all) and I wanted to support the developer, so I went for it when it first released. Overall, I am very satisfied with the game, had a good time, and would buy it again. 

Not having multiple endings doesn't bother me much. If the "choices" are scattered throughout the game, I'm not replaying, solving puzzles I already know the answers too, just to change a couple of dialogue options. The same thing for if the choice is at the end and there's no individual save feature for me to go back to. I think it's fair to expect an indie developer to just make a game that's fun to play once. There's dialogue options that don't really matter, but I found the characters you interact with the most really endearing and felt connected very quickly.

I'm [i]really[/i] glad to have a game like this where the story isn't just "surveillance bad".

The mechanics are good though sometimes it can be hard to scan things even when you know what to scan. Special ways to solve problems are generally only used once and can be decently complex and fun because of that. They're usually a refreshing change and can be [i]incredibly[/i] intense. I just wish certain things would be randomized between attempts.

Now for the story. Like I said, I'm very glad it didn't go for the usual story this type of game attracts. It's a fairly decent plot with likeable, well voiceacted characters and let's you figure out certain things early without being utterly obvious.

The problem is the ending. The rest will be in spoilers, though I'm not gonna say anything specific. This is basically just for people that are really adverse to any kind spoiler, no matter how small.

"The Operator" is an incredibly enjoyable experience that draws you deep into the world of digital investigation and conspiracy. As an operator for the FDI, I found myself thoroughly engrossed in solving complex cases, and the game kept me on the edge of my seat from start to finish.

Pros:

Engaging Mechanics: The investigative tools are a highlight of the game. Analyzing evidence, digging through databases, and assisting field agents in real-time was so satisfying that I often wished I had more time to use these tools.

Gripping Narrative: Each case is a well-crafted story with twists and turns that kept me hooked. Although I figured out the major twist halfway through, it was set up nicely and added to the overall tension rather than detracting from it.

Atmospheric Tension: The game excels at creating a sense of paranoia and urgency. The mysterious presence of the cyber criminal HAL and the cryptic messages to "trust no one" added layers of psychological depth that kept me fully engaged. There's one part of the game that had me sweating buckets because it was so tense, but I won’t spoil anything—just be prepared!

Cons:

Not Enough Time with the Tools: My only real gripe is that the game could have given us more opportunities to dive deeper into the mechanics. The tools are so well-designed that I wanted to spend even more time exploring their capabilities.

A Bit Short: The game is on the shorter side, but considering it was developed by a very small team (possibly just one or two people), what they’ve created is nothing short of incredible. I sincerely hope to see more from them in the future.

Anyone who appreciates immersive narratives and detective games should definitely play this one. The game provides an exciting experience with tough puzzles and a gripping narrative that will keep you wondering. Although some may find the twist predictable, it's skillfully done and doesn't take away from the overall experience. Even with its length, it's an amazing accomplishment for such a small team, and I can't wait to see what they come up with next.

This is not really the case, even though you could really batch it with it and Obra Dinn as point & click made for people prejudicied against point & click, The Operator have more stronger emphasis on its narrative over the actual case solving.

This probably no biggest departure between what you could expect compared to what the game delivers so it's probably what needs to be the clearest : this isn't some X-files case solving about solving stranges cases and chasing aliens, this is short narrative game. While I kinda wish it had more filler cases, that would require to use all the different tools to solve, it's clearly outside the scope of this game. The story itself is a very typical thriller, to the point is possible to get where it's trying to go just because the trope used are that common and maybe it would a problem if this was a visual novel.

The obvious gimmick here is the entire game is told through the screen of a computer, a very limited dispositive that get the most out of the very conventional plot. This may sound dismissive thriller are very codified type of story, that's part of the interest in even saying "this is a thriller", the same way I expect to see a group of young people sharing their sob stories and their way to save the world in my J-RPG. So how do you make something like this interesting when you can't hire Keanu Reeves to do cool stuff on screen ? What the Operator does is giving as little as possible. Low quality camera footage, damaged photography, unreliable testimony, chat windows and a lot of phone calls, an quick acces to a lot clues but very little interaction with the actual narrative. Backed-up by the dynamic soundtrack, this game creates some pretty sincere moment of tension. Especially when the main character position matches the player playing the game, good for immersion even if you don't emphasize too much with the character (I didn't really, sorry).

I do think this game overall is a bit short and lack a bit of substance as an investigation game, but is a narrative game really dedicated to its theme.

The game kind of struggles with what it actually wants you to do and who it wants you to be.

To get started: I really wanted to love this game, because I like researching and playing detective. However you are given a set of tools and expectations to be resourceful, while actually non of it works outside the main storyline. 

As a package it is nicely crafted and for a while it has you engaged, but at some points it expects you to really take control and go beyond the objective ... but only in the exact path the developer(s) have set out for you. The developer(s) haven't realized that it becomes very frustrating, very fast that the game doesn't allow you to explore or make combinations other than that what they exactly have programmed you to do. So encouraging you to think beyond one case, but at the same time limiting your possibilities very much gets your frustrated easily. Sure there is a subpath that you miss sometimes, but you only miss it because all your other attempts to try something different aren't supported (like you can't call anyone on your own or analyse something that isn't supposed to be analyzed). If you don't have any room to play / experiment, you stop doing it and than at some point the game will make fun of you and point out that you have missed something.

Same goes for the dialogs. The game keeps asking you to select an answer while none of it really matters, it is all linear! Again it learns you to make choices, but the choices don't matter so why are they even there than? Just for a single different line of text to go back to the main story path again?

I'll try to give it a go some more when I am less frustrated. But for now, it has got me fed up.

The polish of the game also stands out with the brilliant sound design. The music is spot-on with some Tool-like guitars like the song Rosetta Stoned blended with futuristic suspense tunes.

Moreover, the game has its audio cues timed to the millisecond; they don't feel like jump scares but like actual sound design choices. The audio cues ALWAYS enhance the experience in this game, which was fascinating to experience.

Played the demo and got really hooked, so I bought the game the next day full price.

AFTER the demo I expected it to be very similar to Orville and Cyber Manhunt, with the primary focus on using the game's mechanics to solve multiple criminal cases, most unrelated or maybe filler and some interconnected into a bigger picture.
It was... kinda like that? But instead of a focus on multiple cases and the solving mechanics, it focuses solely on one storyline.

Which to me was actually really sad I guess because the gameplay mechanics were really well implemented and would have made for a super nice gameplay loop but instead got used once to advance the plot and then got discarded (e.g. the lab analysis or manually unlocking files). 

Also, the game is probably 75% dialogue, in which you are given choices that lead nowhere. You feel like your choices should matter, maybe in resulting in different endings but there is only one ending implemented. It actually made me compare it more to a visual novel than a detective game.

The lack of "filler cases" is also more of a negative in this particular storyline. I've read that the developer wanted to focus more on the main story instead of filler but I think some filler would've helped the player to immerse themselves better into their role, made better usage of the well-implemented mechanics and would've allowed the player to connect with the characters better, settle mentally on the twists and turns of the main story and process them before the next thing gets thrown at them. It felt very fast-paced with no breathing time from basically the get-go and if I'm not mistaken the story takes place within only a couple of days in-game which also does not seem realistic.

Conclusion:
+ well-made from a technical point of view
+ well implemented mechanics
+ good soundtrack
- poor use of mechanics
- unclear advertisement (detective game vs. very story-driven, more of a visual novel)
- no actual choices made by the player even though it feels like they should have mattered
- lack of cases with a rather short gameplay time as a result
- lots of dialogue with comparatively little gameplay

If you're looking for somethin akin to Orville, Cyber Manhunt or even Her Story, this is not it.
I considered requesting a refund but I believe that if I buy a product, receive it and use it, there is no reason in refunding it, even if it was not what I expected

This is a tough one for me to review. On the one hand, this is a very cool concept, and I think it’s executed very well. On the other, it feels very much like a proof of concept for a bigger game. 

I don’t want to get into spoilers, but I will say that I would’ve liked a few more “normal” cases to solve before jumping into the government conspiracy aspect. I feel like it would’ve made some of the later reveals stand out more. As it stands, you start the game immediately suspecting something is fishy. Your very first case kicks off the game-long mystery. 

Also, I feel like some of the reveals were done more for the immediate shock value than they were for actual plot reasons. As in, you uncover a number of secrets that feel like they don’t actually go anywhere, beyond the initial stomach-dropping “oh shit” moment. 

I would love to see this expanded upon in a sequel, which is why I’m ultimately recommending this game. The fact that my biggest complaint is that “I wanted more” should ultimately speak to the quality of the experience. Like I said, it’s got good bones. I just wish it had been fleshed out more.

I bought the game to unravel mysteries as an FBI operative—a game I could play for several hours. The gameplay mechanics are exactly what I was hoping for, but unfortunately, some of them are only used once throughout the entire game.
The story is extremely short, with a plot that becomes obvious within the first 40 minutes of gameplay. Seriously, 2 hours of gameplay for 14€? Not to meantion an "Original Soundtrack" for another 10€. If players could skip some dialogues and cutscenes, the game would only last 30 minutes. The story feels more like a detective TV show where everything is "weird," "doesn't make sense," and "everything is interconnected."

In summary:
+ The game mechanics are awesome! - Unfortunately, their potential is wasted on a simplistic story with a soap-opera-like plot seen more than thousands of times on TV.
+ The soundtrack (not bought), sound effects, and voice acting are excellent.
- The story is simple and feels rather sloppy (95% of the ideas went into coding and mechanics, 5% into the story). Perhaps it's due to the potential for a speedrunning community?
- When I calculate the "price per hour" of the main story, this game is undoubtedly the worst in my entire game library (7€ per hour (almost 12€ if you buy the "original soundtrack"), including cutscenes and dialogues).
- The game has unskippable cutscenes (returning home), dialogues (the tutorial), and end credits, likely so that you can’t get a refund within the 2-hour Steam policy.
? If the sequel to this game will also be only 2 hours long, the developers might as well not even bother. It’s not worth the money.

If the game was a bit longer (at least 4 hours of a decent story), I would recommend it, but unfortunately, I can't.
Definitely buy it during a sale, just not now.

I have to say I was absolutely hooked with the concept of [i] The Operator. [/i] One watch of the trailer will tell you why; an operator helping with government investigations, analyzing clues, basically being the man-in-the-chair? It's all awesome! But what killed the mood for me was the cliche writing, amateur voice acting, and the simplistic puzzles. First of all the writing. Who TALKS like this?! Every person you meet is quippy, chippy, or clever with their line delivery. These don't sound like professional field agents, they sound like cartoon characters. A man has been killed, TAKE THIS SERIOUSLY! They should be more realistic, a bit grittier, more direct. And why am I doing everything? What exactly is your job here??

Next are the puzzles. They are already simple enough, but I feel babied and talked down to by the characters we meet. The game would make itself so much more compelling if there were harder applications! Something I had to grill through to find what my agent needed. So far, I can click two buttons and get the answer to the riddle. I don't [i] feel [/i] like a secret agent, which is what I bought the game for. And not to mention the game's animations for security footage, which are taken so seriously for how poor in quality they are. The tone simply doesn't match. 

Finally, I had a sincerely hard time caring about the story of the game. The plot was mildly interesting, conspiracies and hackers and whatnot, but it didn't land. Mainly because it meant wading through monologues from the characters, which drove me insane. If the game was harder, there would be much more to invest in. I would feel accomplished! But after completing the first two days, I feel like there was no other option but to succeed. There was never any risk of me failing, which made it hard for me to connect to the game at all. In the end it was not the experience I was expecting, and if you're looking to be a tech-savvy sleuth, look elsewhere.
