[h1] Short and fun little deep state conspiracy game [/h1] 

First of all, this game is short.[b] VERY SHORT [/b]. It takes about 3-4 hours to complete, but the game tells the story it wants to tell in that time so it´s fine. 

[h3] Story 7/10 [/h3] 
The story is fine. It starts of strong, leaving you as the operator to figure out what you are doing and why you are doing it.
As soon as the story picks up the pace, the game is beginning to get more and more predictable. Sure, it makes sure to tell the story in a convincing way, but if the player has had any contact with books that follow similar plotlines or watched a few "rogue agent fighting conspiracy" movies you know where the plot is going and how the game will end. Ending was fine, a bit disappointing because the cut was fast and hard and resulted in a cliff hanger. To me it feels like the devs wrote a story thats about 10 hours long and just cut the game in half when they had the opportunity to do so, preparing the player for a future sequel.

[b] STORY SPOILERS [/b]
[spoiler] In my opinion the reveal that Mike Trench, our friend and FDI director, is the mole and head of the "Operator Program" was very predictable about half-way through  the game (ever since the Biolab incident and the player operator talking about "baiting out the mole"). The Ghost was written in a very stereotypical bad guy hitman way: I dont have a name, my identity was erased. I know the truth but can not tell you. You can ask any question as long as it is not "out of bounds". Yeah, very corny and kinda cringy. In general, even though the way it is written is good and convincing for the most part, sometimes the game feels like the devs wanted to take the easy way out in a few situations (Player being Sasha Cole, Xavier actually being a friend of HAL, the Ghost just escaping like nothing happened and being able to interfere with HALs scripts...) But hey, for what it is, it´s a solid experience. [/spoiler] 

[h3] Music 7/10 [/h3] 
Pretty good, especially the main menu music. But not memorable. Just nice BGM. Not really worth paying for the OST imo but who am i to decide.

For me the games strong points are the art direction or visual direction in combination with the player interacting with the desktop. It really immerses you in your role as the operator and you really feel like you are investigating CCTV footage and sifting through documents to find small clues. The game really takes you out of this illusion by having to click the objective and then clicking the requested information. Not a fan of that, could have been integrated in a more smooth and immersive way. Audio design is great too, the voice acting feels believable enough and the sound effects are accurate and synced well. Nothing really to complain about there.

Overall it is a fun, short and interesting game with a few flaws that can be overlooked. Wait for a sale before you buy it though, for 3-4 hours of playtime it is just a bit too much (About 1€/$ per hour of playtime should be standard imo).

I bought this game hoping to find a Spycraft (1996) successor, after already beating the two Orwell games, and liking them, but hungry for a more realistic Cold War setting. In a way I was satisfied by The Operator, even if it is a really short game and consequently some story elements are rather simplistic and not well furthered. Some investigation tools are rather cool to use, but unfortunately, for the major part, you use them just once. Some sequences are very tense, like a bomb defusal where you need to read an operative manual and defuse the explosive in 20 minutes. Or another one where you give directions to an agent on the field while looking through a surveillance camera system. But you can't fail at them, this is not an hard game and you just need to solve the puzzles in a linear way to proceed further into the story. Which is not really strong or particulary original, but I liked the final plot twist, which saved it for me exactly when I started to feel bored and uninterested.

As you can see, for every aspect of the game I liked, there is something else I found underwhelming. It is not a bad game but I don't think it can reach the first Orwell game or my favorite title in this genre, Spycraft, from nearly 30 years ago. I will give it a 6, and recommend it anyway, because I would like to see more games in this genre and historical period. Maybe the author will be able to work on a sequel and refine some aspects of it. Meanwhile I'll wait for a real Spycraft successor, let's hope I don't have to wait for another 30 years :|

Let's start with the obvious as soon as you start the game : the sound design, musics, sound effects, ambiance and voice acting are *gorgeous*. And it gets better with time.

Yet I'm debating to put a thumb up or down. On the one hand, it's original and well made with an impressive level of finition. On pretty much every aspect.
On the other hand ... I don't believe a game is the proper vector for this experience. The gaming aspects constantly break the immersion (at least for me), which in turn ruin any tension or engagement towards the plot, as I view it from a game point of view. For instance, you're in a conversation with someone, yet can take the time to do whatever background checks you want and the person will kindly wait as long as you want before you answer. All of this make the events less impactful emotionnally. I'd add to that a deep insatisfaction with the ending (not as much the content of it as the unfinished business that stops abruptly), and the frustration of sometimes not doing the things right, but still having to deal with the consequences. Yes, it's more immersive, but it makes the gaming experience more frustrating, and I don't want to restart the whole game, so I have a feeling of unfinished business. Not in a branching story game way, more like losing a level but having to go on instead of restarting.

To sum up in a single sentence : the gaming aspects are in the way of the immersion, and the immersion is in the way of the gaming enjoyment.

+++ Sound design
++ Global quality and realism
+ A few good ideas and tools thrown into the mix for variety
- The end, with multiple untied ends
- Too short, with a lack of reusability of the tools and 'sandbox' aspect (you're very handheld at all times)
-- The inadequate mix of immersion and gaming

----Experience the perfect blend of thrilling storytelling, engaging puzzles, and fully voice-overed gameplay in The Operator. ----

The Operator is an engaging and innovative game where you step into the shoes of an operator assisting field agents in gathering intelligence. The core gameplay revolves around analyzing various pieces of evidence, including video material, audio fragments, and documents, to provide crucial information to the agents on the ground. This puzzle-solving aspect hits the sweet spot, offering a challenge that is neither too easy nor overly difficult, making it enjoyable for a wide range of players.

One of the game's standout features is its story. As you progress through the puzzles, a compelling narrative unfolds, complete with a plot twist that keeps you on the edge of your seat. The blend of story and gameplay is seamless, making each task feel significant and tied to the larger narrative.

For a price of 13 euros, The Operator offers excellent value. The story is gripping (which is btw fully voiced overed!), the puzzles are well-designed, and the overall experience is thoroughly satisfying. The game’s length is also perfect; I completed it in about 3.5 hours, making it ideal for a long gaming session or spread over a weekend.

In summary, The Operator is a great blend of storytelling and puzzle-solving. It’s an experience that stands out in the indie game market, offering both a thrilling narrative and engaging gameplay. Highly recommended for those who enjoy a good story and a well-crafted challenge.

Hi, I'm arko, I can give a little bit of backstory;

When I was a younger kid, I always loved the idea of discovering a crime, investigating, solving cases, it just scratched an itch and ideas I had for my brain.

Almost a decade later and I still enjoy such, I love ARG's, and such, and whenever I find one, I try my absolute HARDEST to solve.

I started off with the Kaigan Games, Games, Sara is Missing, popularized in the late 2010's, you take perspective as a person who has found Sara's phone, and tries to investigate by asking her friends, family, and debunk cultist relations. Later on, I moved onto the SIMULACRA series, though not totally investigative games, they follow a similar principle, I loved SIMULACRA 1, and replayed it 4 times. It just satisfied me a way other games have not.

I found out about this game way before release, I became excited to purchase it, though I did not buy it day one, I bought it extremely early. This game, scratched an itch no other games I listed prior and ARG's that I didn't even know existed. 

The way the game functions, the calls, everything that's in this game, is great. I love the operating system, and I think this is by far one of the best interpretations of a call center in the 80's-2000's. Everything from the keyboard sounds, the ambiance behind you, the mouse clicking, the computer effect, is so immersive, and I believe this is one of the most immersive games, I have ever played.

-----------------------------------------------------

My opinions on the story, there will be spoilers.

You start off the game with a cutscene, you are being questioned by someone in an absurdly bright white room, there's nothing there but white. At first, you will think this cutscene means nothing, and is useless, but at the end, it will totally blow your mind, I won't say it here, as I want YOU to experience the thrill and twists this game has to offer. 

The immersive and keep you on your toes gameplay, especially with the bomb you have to deal with to make sure an Agent doesn't die, the back and forth with the notepad, manual, call, commands, is extremely thrilling, and keeps you nervous and anxious, as one wrong move, will kill the person you are trying to save.

The use of a system that has a database, is great, scanning cars, people, places, and objects to help solve cases is amazing, and I believe it is the best yet.

-------------------------------------

For example, at the beginning, I tried to resist and wanted to shout, "Catch Hal!" I even tried making unauthorized ip-calls to my superiors to report Hal via the terminal, but the game didn't allow such actions. This is a big downside for me. I want to make my own decisions rather than choosing from a set of predetermined responses. The game doesn't even offer the illusion of choice.

All puzzles have only one solution, and that doesn't work for me.

There are cases though where I noticed things and the game treated me as if I hadn't - suggesting moments where the Devs perhaps thought they were being cleverer than they were.

I finished it in 2hr 48mins and did enjoy it, the price is acceptable for the quality I feel but the game deserves and desperately needs a bigger sequel with more cases and replyability and perhaps a small discount for those of us who bought the first proof of concept game.

I am the fan of the stories in games, and "The Operator" has just reached the top with this engaging storyline. What made it so cool is that the plot was very catchy, so it kept me playing. I could only wish for more depth in some storylines, making them way more complicated and detailed. Just a few more levels of detail in the story would make the experience even more puzzling and immersive. 

The game needs the possibility of side tasks that would help to. It would provide depth to the experience and variety of mundaneness, because otherwise, having some really mundane cases that are not related to the main story might make it feel more real and alive. The game mechanics were great! Simple and comprehensible, suitable for many players. My only complaint is that the game felt a bit too short.

Something like statistics about what choices I made would be great; for instance, what percentage of the other players made the same decisions. That would be a great addition concerning interactive replay. The user interface in the game, especially the terminal interface, was so awkward in the context of the end of the 1990s since it felt very modern. A more period-appropriate design would add to the overall sense of immersion and give a more authentic feeling to the game. All in all, "The Operator" is quite a compelling game with a good story and intuitive mechanics.

The biggest problem with The Operator for me is that it all falls apart just as it was gaining momentum. The last set of puzzles lack the sense of discovery from earlier, the game abruptly ends leaving a bunch of unanswered questions, and you're left feeling like nothing you did mattered.

If you want to feel like you're an investigator for the US government in an agency like the FBI or CIA, this game puts you there. It's more than a visual novel, but less than a full-fledged world with practically infinite choices.

Even so, it feels full and like the choices matter. Definitely some memorable moments in this. I would like a full-fledged game with many choices and outcomes, but that would deserve a higher price tag. This is what it should be for the price, and isn't too short.

The story is solid and engaging. Having worked in the government, I can say this is idealized a bit, but is definitely not ridiculous compared to crime shows. I was surprised at several points in the plot, and the way you discover the protagonist's situation and that he encounters is solid.

However, there are a few things that make it a bit realistic. It is set in the early 90s, yet the "FDI" (not FBI) have the capability to "enhance" photos like Stable Diffusion can now. There are cell phone towers and tracking, but not many people used cell phones in the US back at that time, and the ones that did had big Motorolla boxes the size of a lunch box they plugged into. They were technically mobile, but not very. The cell phone antenna had to be attached to the car roof with a magnet. And it cost over $100/mth. Sure, it wasn't uncommon for business people, and really rich people had somewhat smaller mobile phones, but still.

Also, in the boot screen, it shows a version of Linux that is "x86_64", but 64 bit didn't become really common until around 2007.

However, you can forgive these small foibles since you can consider the game as a parallel universe world; very similar, but slightly different, like how you work for the FDI instead of FBI. Perhaps in this world, they had a decade or two jump on us in technology.

I thoroughly enjoyed this and hope they put out a longer game with either more choice or perhaps getting to play more characters, or a single protagonist through a longer story arc. When it comes down to it, my only complaint with this game is that there wasn't more of it. That's a good complaint to have if it matches up with a good price, and it does. Good luck to the dev team now and in the future!

The good is that it’s quite a good experience, even if the puzzles are simple and intuitive, they’re not repetitive, and there’s some variety to it. The plot is extremely well written and serves well the thematics of the game.

The bad is that I feel like somethings were underdeveloped. I’m referring specifically to the puzzles, I think like at least the chemical compound/molecules breaking could have appeared a couple more times. Not only that, I think the puzzles could experience a little bit more of variety, like 1-2 more types of puzzles. Although the plot was great, it also could have dived a bit further.

The ugly is how the story breaks on the climax to an open ending. The story was just building up throughout the first two hours. During the 3rd hour, it was building the suspense to the climax, and then it’s just ends abruptly. The game could be double its playtime and still have room for a sequel, if the developers/publishers wanted to sell more content later on, during the next couple months (through a DLC) or down the road. However, the story is unfinished. It does leave mixed feelings like many are referring down on the comments and on their reviews.

It sort of starts that way, but doesn't stay that way for long. It's VERY linear as far as I can tell, and while I think there are different outcomes based on player inputs, I have yet to try that. It's not the investigation game it's labeled as. It's still well put together and thought out, but I felt a little bit misled, as there is really only one single "case" that you're working on as the player, it just happens to include a few other cases that you work on in the tutorial stages. 

Without spoiling it, I think it's a good game, though I don't know if I would pay full price for it. I think if you could get it for under $10 USD it would be a much better value, personally. But, we'll see how it goes on the replay-ability of the game and that might change. I'm curious how different actions and responses affect the outcome of the game for sure. 

Soundtrack really buffed this game a lot too, it was really well timed and well orchestrated. 

My main complaint is some of the cutscenes are ridiculously long for what their substance is. There is basically no substance to most of them, it's just some sound effects and maybe the occasional spot of dialogue.

As someone else said in their review, it scratched an itch I didn't know I had, but I would've been much more excited to see some real investigating. Like phasmophobia, but you're the computer geek at this government intelligence agency. If you play through the first hour or so, you'll see sort of what I mean by that.

The Operator is one of the games that show the limitations of Steam's "Yes/No" model for review. It's a good game, it's solid, but it's got its limitations that you need to understand before you buy.

To put it briefly: The Operator is the videogame equivalent of a good B-movie thriller. As a puzzle game and narrative experience it "does the job". You will get about four hours worth of puzzles that are just difficult enough to make you feel smart, but nothing that is designed to resist you too long either. You'll get a scenario that follows the codes of the conspiracy thriller, but is strongly linear and doesn't do anything you haven't seen at least a few times before...

There are puzzle games out there that will make you forever regret that you aren't able to experience them for the first time once more. Obra Dinn, There is No Game, Chants of Sennaar...The Operator is not one of those. It hits all the right notes, but the performance isn't inspiring.

If you like the genre of puzzle and thriller, then by all means go for it. It is a good, solid game for those gamers whose expectations are appropriately set. But if you haven't played puzzle games for a while and are looking for an amazing, unforgettable experience? Try the others first and come back here when you're hooked to the genre.

While a very polished and well-crafted experience, this game has a number of fatal flaws that undermine and eventually irrevocably cripple your enjoyment of it.  Firstly, it's incredibly short.  I do understand that this tends to be the case for these kinds of games, crafting content for them is much more effort intensive than it is for other genres, but even by the standards of other games in this genre, you get very little playtime compared to its cost.  This is further exacerbated by a complete lack of replay value, as the story is completely linear and has no alternate endings, though there are a few pieces of content not central to the story that the player can find through their own initiative.  If you take nothing else from this review and do decide to buy the game, buy it on sale, the existing content doesn't really justify the price point.

To get into the real reasons this is a negative review, as money alone wouldn't have been enough to get me to write this, we need to first revisit the game's linearity.  The game does provide the illusion of choice, but none of the choices the player can make matter, and acting as though they do will inevitably see the game yanking on your leash and railroading you back to the single story it wants to tell.  This linearity continues to the mysteries that form the game's content, as they are designed so that the player is forced to solve them linearly as well.  Rather than providing multiple angles of attack, players must solve one specific part of a mystery before progressing to the next one, so for the most part you don't get that feeling of everything coming together as multiple clues and leads snap together into a single image, though there are exceptions to this.  I can't get too much into the ending without spoiling players, but it was abrupt, unsatisfying, and served to terminate any remaining sense of agency I had.  Everything I had accomplished was undone in an instant, in a way that felt, frankly, disrespectful and contemptuous to me as a player.  The entire point of a game, the thing that fully differentiates it from other forms of media, is that the person consuming it has agency, is not simply a passive observer but actively engages with and shapes the piece of media that they are consuming.  Of all the games I've played, this embraces that principle the least, and suffers for it.

The ultimate sin of The Operator, however, the one no detective game can be forgiven for, is its predictability.  I am in no way talented when it comes to mysteries.  When I play a detective game, read a mystery novel, or watch a movie in those genres, I am generally unable to put together the pieces ahead of time and figure out the twist before it is presented to me.  This was not the case with The Operator.  I was able to determine most of the major narrative twists well ahead of time, because they were fairly obviously telegraphed.  There were a few that were well done, and there were some that would have been very good if other obvious elements hadn't telegraphed them ahead of time.  Anyone playing this game will likely figure out its main narrative twists well before they are presented to the player, and that is truly tragic.

Pros:
Immersion: The narrative takes the lead in the game. As we solve puzzles and analyze evidence, an intriguing story unfolds with unexpected twists. If you like sci-fi plots and conspiracy theories, you'll find the immersion very appealing.
Nostalgia: Dealing with equipment and devices from the 90s is something much appreciated.

Cons:
Short Game: “The Operator” is relatively short compared to other titles. Some players may feel that the experience ends too soon.
Limitations: The game feels very structured and with little freedom of action where decisions are not taken into account. There are times when you feel that you just have to click the mouse and that you can't do anything else.

Conclusion: good concept, good idea, beautiful experience of interacting with computers from other times, but all this feels a bit short.

I can't in good conscience give this game a good review, but I also can't give it a poor review. It's times like this I wish Steam had a middle-ground review option. This game was very fun and scratched an itch I didn't know I had. However, labeling it as an investigation game or describing it the way it does is misleading. Yes, there is some investigation, but there's really only one singular crime to solve. The storyline is very linear and easy to guess. If it were marketed as a game about solving a singular crime, that would be accurate, but it misleads you in the description by stating, 'Investigate mysterious crimes. Use cutting-edge FDI software to dig for clues, solve puzzles, and uncover the truth.' This is incorrect. You only use most of the 'software' exactly once, after implying you should read the extensive manual that comes along with it. This is a game that you could probably finish within 2-3 hours, which also doesn't justify its price. Honestly, they could have dropped the mid-tier storyline and just made a game along the lines of Criminal Minds or CSI, where you use these tools to try to solve cases, and it would be infinitely more fun. I know I'm probably the outlier here with my review, and I will say I did enjoy what they had, but it just wasn't what they promised in their wording and descriptions (maybe I misunderstood some stuff, who knows). There does seem to be an open door for expansions in the future, but if they're along the same timeframe as this game and offer only 2-3 hours of playtime, they should drastically reduce the price because as it stands, it felt like an expensive tech demo.

首先看题材分类就知道不是强调游戏性的作品，所以就当综合作品来评价描述吧
---------------------------------好评内容---------------------------------
1.首先要夸的是风格化的水平还可以，在平面演出上做到了统一以及小部分出彩。
2.惊喜感比较强，对于矛盾叙事不敏感或者游玩心情较为轻松的玩家来说，能够在不同章节的不同节点给出惊喜感，且节奏把握能力也不错，将玩家体验的游戏内几个简单系统控制在了刚好不会厌烦的程度。
3.结构简单清晰，五脏俱全：卡关的引导思考恰到好处。
4.谜题难度分布合理，作品中的解谜交互要素的难度比较梯度，部分要素比较新颖。
---------------------------------不足之处---------------------------------
1.对话逻辑：部分人物的行为和对话逻辑难以自圆其说。
2.程序的判断逻辑有优化之处：对话需要经过A再到B才能触发进程，然而玩家拥有直接选择B的能力，这类强制玩家操作顺序的情况会一定程度上影响体验。
3.许多人提到的问题：分支对话无意义，也就是对话系统本身无法对剧情起到关键性分支作用，本身系统其实也是支持这种功能，但或许因为工期等其他缘故，制作组并没有加入这些内容。（或许拆弹专家是一个实验）

I'm usually not a fan of dialogue choices and multiple endings, so I didn't know how to feel when I found out this game [i]doesn't[/i] have alternative endings.  Like another user put it, it really felt like I had reached the "bad ending", and that I was supposed to make different choices.  But playing through a second time did not change the outcomes aside from slightly different dialogue, and seeing one or two subtle hints I had missed the first time around.

And the developer has confirmed that it's not intended to be replayable (see the dev's [url=https://steamcommunity.com/app/1771980/discussions/0/4511002214535949429/]community post[/url])

The interface is quite well done, with a variety of technical mechanics.  The in-game documents and user manuals are quite impressively believable in style, while staying relevant to the gameplay, and to the storyline.  I quite enjoyed the [spoiler]"Keep Talking and Nobody Explodes"[/spoiler] style puzzle.

I was a little disappointed that the terminal was so limited, but given this is a relatively small game, that's understandable.

At times, especially at the start, it felt like a bit of information overwhelm moving too quickly, but it generally seems to be quite forgiving (though I haven't tested what happens if you don't answer a call, or fail to [spoiler]defuse the bomb[/spoiler]).

Often it felt a bit too heavy on the handholding.  [spoiler]The "watch me."  "Are you watching me?" prompts for the scripted surveillance made me giggle[/spoiler].  Most of the big reveals were heavily hinted at early on so I knew long before the characters themselves knew.  There were a couple that surprised me though.

The voice acting was quite good.  As was the sound design, and animations.  There's quite a few unskippable animations but they're generally done quite well and relevant to the storyline or puzzles.

Overall decent little game.  First playthrough took me just about under ~6hrs at a meandering pace (and not keeping track of breaks).  Would play a sequel if it's ever made.

The Operator is what I would describe as a psychological spy/detective thriller where you investigate crimes. Quite honestly, what you see on the store is what you get. The atmosphere (early-mid 1990s) is fantastic and does a great job immersing you into the world. The story is very good (albeit a bit short) so I won't go into much detail about it. That said, the moment(s) of realization actually did surprise me more than I expected, especially later on in the story (I'm sure fellow players remember their experience realizing the thing about [spoiler]THAT camera feed[/spoiler]).

For the game itself, I enjoyed many aspects of it but was somewhat let down by others. The core gameplay loop is quite fun, and it doesn't impede on the storytelling. The largest "disappointment" - also a common theme in fellow reviews - the game is just too darn short. I felt like I went a bit slow, and my playthrough lasted about 3.5 hours. Given the cheap price I felt like it was a good deal, but I think extending it it to maybe 6 hours would make the rising action and climax much more appreciated. The puzzles, while somewhat challenging, varied and engaging, were generally one-trick ponies that I expected to use at least one or two more times during the game.

Would I recommend this game? Yes. Despite it being shorter than I expected, I still feel like I paid a good price for a well-written thriller story that I could tell had a lot of love put into it. I'm hoping the devs make another game like this that's more meaty with the game content and length, I would definitely purchase it.

review:
Really enjoyed this! I've read some criticisms about the length and the ending, but for me both of those were perfect. It's nice to play a complete game in a few hours sometimes.

The mystery and puzzle solving aspects were pitched well and kept me guessing throughout and it hit all the right 90s X-Files buttons.

It took me about 3 hours to complete, but I didn't feel it was too short or long. Some people are unhappy that it ends on a sort of downer cliffhanger ending, but to me it was the perfect ending for a story of faceless government conspiracies. The ending hints at a continuation anyway, and I'm up for that.

My only real criticism is that I didn't really like the blurry cutscenes. I understand the aesthetic choice for those, but I just felt they were too long overall, when they should have just been short transitions from one scene to another.

review:
I don't write many reviews and this one is more of a warning in some ways. 

This is much more of a click along adventure with a couple of mini games. I haven't replayed the game to see if the solutions to the mini games are random or fixed. But i purchased the game after playing the demo and that definitely felt like the game would involve much more gameplay and hard work, perhaps some red herrings and a chance to fail.

It is hard to give a proper review of the game without ruining it for people, but it is very short. The slow delivery of text communications or waiting on videos to play pads it out considerably at times and it does feel deliberate to lengthen the game especially at times when there is tension and i personally felt i would be doing things much faster if i had been allowed.

Now don't take that the wrong way, i suspect most people who complain it is short were wanting more. Even if you work out the twists before they come it is worth getting to the end, though it does feel a bit disappointing when you already worked out the big reveals early on. And yes if you look carefully you will at least suspect very early in the game what some outcomes will be. 

Over all the game concept and execution is good, i would have preferred more puzzles or having to dig a bit more for solutions to problems, you are given tools you use exactly once and then never have to use again. It feels set up for a sequel and i hope that they do make one with a longer story.

If you are looking for a click along movie and enjoy that type of game then it may be worth full price to you.
If you are looking for a complex puzzle game where you are the one solving things wait till it is on sale but still get it.

My recommendation is heavily conditional. If you are into conspiracies and point-and-click games with simple puzzle elements, I would recommend this at around $10. If you don't fall into those categories, then you aren't the target demographic and I can't recommend it. Overall Operator is not a bad game - in fact, I would really like to see more content for this, or perhaps even more games like it - but it's held back by a few flaws.

First, The Good:
[list]
    [*]The setting and overall theme is great. You play as a deskbound investigator at the not-FBI, using your computer to sift through clues and work with field agents to investigate crimes. Naturally, this leads to uncovering conspiracies and shadowy organizations.
    [*]The gameplay is intuitive and accessible. You will never have to pixel-hunt for your clues; when you're inspecting a piece of evidence, the things that your gut tell you are important to the case usually are, and they're usually clickable.
    [*]The story is fun, interesting, and will keep you engaged. It references some real-world "conspiracies" that actually happened.
    [*]The gameplay loop feels fresh. I know games in this format have been done before, but it's been a while since I've seen it executed like this. I don't know of many recent games that are quite like it.
[/list]

Next, The Bad:
[list]
    [*]The puzzles are a bit simple. At times it feels like more of a visual novel than a detective/investigation game.
    [*]Many of the plot twists are predictable. The dramatic reveals towards the end of the game didn't land with me at all because I had already seen them coming way ahead of time.
    [*]Sometimes there are clues that fall into your lap a little too easily, to the point where it doesn't feel believable. The most egregious example: [spoiler]During one investigation, you find the buried body of a scientist who worked on a secret government project. The people involved with the project had him killed to keep him quiet. For some reason, they buried him in a marked grave, near the marked graves of a hundred of the project's victims, wearing his full lab coat, with his work ID showing full name and place of employment still in a cord around his neck, and with unwiped floppy disks in his pocket that contained all of his research and notes.[/spoiler]
    [*]The game is filled with anachronisms. It's supposed to be set in 1992, but it doesn't even attempt to maintain this setting. Everybody has a cell phone, which in the 90s were expensive, rare, and had very limited coverage; the computer used by main character appears to have a multi-core CPU, which didn't exist until the 2000s; and one of the early investigations involves a digital camera with a large preview screen, which also did not exist in 1992. All of this is like having a character use an iPhone in a video game about Operation Desert Storm; it can be immersion-breaking. Operator probably should have been set in the mid- to late-2000s, not 1992.
    [*]At the time of writing, there is only one ending, and it feels rushed. [spoiler]Outside of one minor detail regarding a side character, your choices don't matter.[/spoiler]
    [*]The last and most obvious drawback is probably the one you've seen mentioned in other reviews: this is a short game. It'll probably only take you around 3 hours to complete. The cynic in me wonders if this was done intentionally to get around the 2-hour Steam refund limit.
[/list]

I did enjoy my time with Operator; if you're like me, and enjoy the thought of playing detective and uncovering government conspiracies, you probably will too. Ultimately I think this is a decent game with a solid concept behind it, but the problems I listed above hold me back from recommending this unconditionally. In particular, I feel that Operator is slightly overpriced when measured against the amount of gameplay time you're likely to get out of it. This seems to be the developer's first game, so I'm hoping that they take the lessons learned from Operator and continue to improve on this formula.

"The Operator" is a good game, except it isn't actually a game... It is more of an interactive film, where your choice doesn't actually matter, for example, despite several attempts to play for the agency, I couldn't do so, you always have to side with some renegade hacker("HAL"). The game just locks in dialogue options, so you can only comply to progress further in the game. When she reveals her identity, you can't report her, which proves how choice doesn't matter in this game, even the dialogue options aren't that much of a choice, as the respondents largely react similarly. Also, many actions in it don't have consequences, like you can mess up all the tasks hundreds of times, and the game just tells you you are wrong, not the characters, the game, like, you can (in some cases) just blindly click the screen and eventually you will get it right. Or with how you can mess up the bomb diffusal and subsequently kill a federal agent, with no consequences. 
Generally, the game is well made, and I have not found any bugs, but the crippling lack of player agency, and no consequences for wrong choices just make the game unplayable, and I would, therefore, not recommend it to other people, as a game at least. As I said, this isn't a game it is an interactive activity, that uses the mechanics of a game.

developer_response:
Hello, thanks for your feedback!

I'm sorry that you felt frustrated by the duration of the game. I spent 3 years developing the game and I prefered to squeeze as much quality as possible, instead of having lower quality content just to add some duration there.
For the price, I hear what you say but I saw this game a bit like a movie. When you go see or buy a movie, you have 1h30/2h for at least 12$. And we wanted to focus on the story and plot twists, to make the "first playthrough" great. I thought that replayability wouldn't be super interesting because you already know the better parts of the game (twists, story and puzzles), and didn't focused too much on this aspect. Again, I'm sorry for that, and I'm glad you still enjoyed the time your spent on the game.

Insanely good. In something of a trend started last week by my playthrough of Anger Foot, "this could have been an email, but you wrote an essay, and an excellent one at that". In other words: What could have been a simple gimmick indie that's fun and gone in one hour is turned upside down by excellent production value, which includes: great direction, engaging narrative, amazing atmosphere and voice acting. I couldn't believe how much stuff *goes on* in this game and by the end it felt like taking part in a conspiration-themed deep state thriller and not playing a puzzle solver, and that's despite spending most of the time (*most*) staring at computer screens.

I guess my only complaint is that the story is *only* good and you can see some twists coming from a mile away, but it more than makes up for that with excellent characters and being, well, engaging on a surprising level. The Operator is also not as open-ended as it seems to be, and could use a few more notable decisions or alternate endings.

Give this a go, there's much more to this title than meets the eye. Heck, if nothing else comes up this can be my personal GOTY.

I did enjoy The Operator, but it's very much one of those titles I wish I could give a sideways thumb to. I can't explain why without spoilers, so I'll tag that section.

This is one of those games that takes place entirely in menus, but still manages to have a compelling story with some puzzling that keeps you engaged in relatively simple game play systems by making you use the analytical parts of your brain. Taking place in a fictional early 1990s where people have cell phones and wireless Internet access, you're playing as a remote operator at the Not FBI who is tasked with helping field agents analyze data relevant to their cases. As you progress, you'll start to become embroiled in a huge conspiracy that goes through many elements of the agency and other places as well. The interface is nice, the music is good and the voice acting of the characters is actually great. If you like stuff that's more action focused, this might not be for you, but I was kept engaged throughout.

Non-specific spoilers and attached criticisms below:

[spoiler]Unfortunately, this game is really let down by it's in my opinion, pretty awful ending. Things come to a head very quickly and the conclusion is thrown at you over just a couple of minutes and isn't well paced. Things somehow manage to end on both a massive cliffhanger, but also very definitively, making the story unsatisfying and also not necessarily possible to continue in a sequel or expansion. You're introduced to some pretty cool investigative mechanics early on that only ever get used once and you also make many what seem like important choices, but you're given a very strong indication by the end that none of them ultimately mattered, nor impacted the outcome. People have said in the forums that there's little narrative value to additional playthroughs.

As a result, the story goes from intriguing and tense to being a big let down and feels like it was rushed and not fully planned out. This took an otherwise great experience and knocked a lot of wind out of its sails for me.

I still recommend this, but definitely on sale. I'm hoping that the developer puts out some content updates to expand the ending more, but I'm not expecting that.[/spoiler]

I'm pretty conflicted regarding my thoughts on this game, if there was a neutral review that would be my rating. 

On one hand the game is very polished, especially for an indie game. It's OST really sets the mood and switches at the perfect time to give you goosebumps. The mechanics are pretty fleshed out; providing a decent challenge while also not being so hard that would require one to search up guides on them. The story is also really thought out and you will get invested into it very quick.

The unfortunate problem I have with this game is that it's extremely short. You can tell by the average 3 hour playtime in the reviews. Additionally all the content + mechanics that the game will throw at your are pretty much in the trailer. (There's only like 10 cases in total) Additionally, all game choices seems to not divert things from the main ending, which means that the game is not very re-playable. There may be some secrets as hinted by the credits achievement or that can be activated by a certain specific sequence of events, but they aren't readily accessible and would require probably some video tutorial guide.

And that leads to the big question, should you buy the game? I honestly can't say in good faith that it is worth it to buy the listed price ($14 USD). If you have a good amount of spare money to spend on games, then go for it. But for most people, I'd recommend holding out on purchasing the game unless it has a heavy sale.

Honestly a criticism might be that you just dip your toe into a lot of things (chemical analyzer, for example) and then quickly move on to the next case/thing.  I will say the post-work/out-of-computer videos dragged, a bit, by the end of the game.  I understand it as an aesthetic choice but those bits weren't for me.

This is a very short game, you'll be done in 3 hours if you're competent at basic puzzles ~ less if you spam the hint feature.

This is an investigation game, where you're an operator in the FDI (or FBI really), and the investigative features boil down to clicking on images and connecting evidence when asked to do so. There's the odd puzzle, but it isn't particularly difficult ~ the hardest part is a timed segment, which you can get around by pausing the game, as all the information remains on screen anyway.

Really, you're here to play this for the storyline, which is a fairly predictable conspiracy laced, X-files, deep-state mystery. The twists are fairly obvious, but the execution of the story beats/elements are lacking. 

It feels as if the story would have better served from being a bit longer, given more time to stew a bit. There's unnecessary padding, in full blur cut scenes that take place between each 'day', and they seem to exist either for 'atmosphere' or more cynically, just to pad the game out so you go over the 2 hour refund mark. (Your mileage may vary, they did nothing for me but waste time.)

If you're an X-Files fans, or someone who loves conspiracy theories, lizard people behind the scenes (or a flat-Earther, whatever), you'll be right at home here. Otherwise, it is a fairly basic investigative game that doesn't quite nail the key plot points to take it beyond being simply decent.

review:
It's an ok game to kill a couple hours. I'm recommending, because I love that people make these kind of games, but I am a bit disappointed. It's VERY easy. The demo gave me Vigil Cases vibe, but turned out the game has incredibly strong and inescapable hand-holding. It's like Vigil Cases in tutorial mode. I thought I'd be looking through a bunch of databases and burrowing into various documents to find details that would solve cases. In reality I was mostly clicking on the dialogue, where NPCs would tell me exactly what to do, which usually involved no more than opening one file, looking up one name, or following a list of instructions.

There was a lot of lost potential here. Like, there's literally zero point in the terminal: the player never gets to figure out what command they should enter, it's always provided by the NPCs. There's no choice who to call, or what information to tell them, except in a couple places. I counted two cool puzzles that gave you an "Aha" moment, the rest was unfortunately easy and predictable.

In short, if you're looking for something to scratch the 'Golden Idol" or "Roottrees are Dead" itch, I wouldn't get your hopes up.

I have very mixed feelings regarding this game, mostly because the play time is so short at about 3 hours.

The game is a bit of a paradox in that it is incredibly well made, with a level of attention to detail that shows a high degree of passion and care went into making it, while at the same time being incredibly short.   Think of a AAA game with only the first level.  Clearly the quality is top-notch but it's a bit baffling someone would put so much work into something so short.  This makes it almost feel like a long demo.

I really liked most of the game, and there is a level of attention to detail and craftsmanship present that all but the best indy titles usually lack. If there was more story so that the game ran 10-20 hours, it would be an easy 9/10, $40+, best game I've played this year. In it's current state, however, I feel like its worth about $10.

So, given its currently priced at $14, what's my final conclusion?  Tepid recommend.  I loved every minute, but given that there were so few of them, I feel a bit conflicted given the price.

I just really hope to see more in the future from this developer.  Make an Operator 2 with at least 10 hours of runtime, price it at ~$30 and you'll have me banging down your door to play.

Also, for those wondering, the game plays like a linear narrative adventure.  Your choices don't matter, but there is some light puzzling and detective work to keep you engaged. The game seems heavily inspired by Hacknet and Orwell, which is a great thing in my book.

Edit: Oh yes, I should mention it runs flawlessly on Windows 7

(This review contains information that might be considered spoilers for some, so read with caution!)

TL; DR:
It holds your hand throughout the game. The investigative puzzles are immersive, but simple and provides very little challenge. It's short, but you might possible still like it for it's presentation and story. If there was a "lukewarm" rating, I would pick that. But since it's clearly a labor of love, I'm inclined to rate positively.

The longer review:

When I heard of The Operator a few days before launch, I was hoping for something to scratch that Obra Dinn / Curse of the Golden Idol itch. Not very many games manage to make you feel like a proper investigator or makes you feel super clever when you progress, and those two games are the gold standard.

The Operator - unfortunately - is not that game.

The immersion is great. You definitely feel like an operator, scanning photos for details that you then input into various databases to yield result. The interface is exactly how you'd imagine a 90's 'hacker' terminal to look like, complete with a terminal and an official looking 'FBI' interface. The majority of the game is fully voiced with competent actors (for the budget).

Although a very polished and - for its medium - a cinematic experience, gameplay-wise it falls into many of the same pitfalls as other "investigative" games like it. The puzzles are - for the most part, but with notable exceptions - simple, requiring few steps to solve. Your hand is woefully held through each of them and the freedom to make your own deductions are sorely lacking. For the most part the tools required to solve a certain puzzle will appear when needed, and disappear when not needed anymore.

The story is decent and very on-par for such a game. It doesn't fully manage to suck you into the world, however. For one, the main plot felt rushed. You're a new operator working cases, and the very first case you receive is a part of a brewing conspiracy. Every case following that is connected in some way. In my opinion, the game doesn't take it's time to build up the world or the characters before placing you front and center into the main plot thread. 

Some of the major plot twists are extremely predictable, and some of what is presented as a major plot development honestly really isn't. We don't know the involved characters enough to care when the revelation is given to us.
The game also makes the cardinal sin of ending abruptly with no real resolution, most questions left unanswered and a feeling that your actions throughout the game had little impact.

A lot of this comes down to personal tastes, hopes and expectations, however. Chances are you'll like this game for it's good presentation and decent enough puzzles. It's not particularly expensive (though maybe a bit pricey for the estimated game time).

Fun and interesting, The Operator brings the vibes of conspiracy and mystery that is very much along the lines of X-Files. The puzzles are interesting and varied, and all hook together into the narrative.

It's worth playing as it isn't very long. The gameplay concept and execution are really good. The voice acting is pretty decent and makes the visual novel style content engaging to consume in addition to the gameplay mechanics. They have some pretty good tricks to flesh out the experience and make it feel more "real" while still managing to keeping the game very lo-fi...

I think it had a lot more potential than it tapped into. A very common criticism will be linearity and lack of player choice or replayability. There are a few moments where you can alter the outcome of an event that feels like it should have a more meaningful impact on the story, but the impact on the overall narrative is actually very little.  I also feel they were very close to allowing you to play the detective by doing your own extracurricular investigating, but then they sort of throw that out by having a character just be like "I bet you didn't notice THIS!" It's like... actually I did notice it and I wanted to have my moment of feeling like a genius. I think this is something that the Ace Attorney games do a little better.... while still railroading you into a very specific solution and solution path, they at least make you feel like you figured things out and make it feel rewarding. I think this game could have done at least more of that if not going as far as to actually add in more optional discovery and unprompted use of the information you gathered.

I'll also say that while this is a pretty good standalone narrative game concept, it feels like something I'd like to see integrated into a bigger game that doesn't play exclusively like this.

Firstly, I'd like to preface my review, by saying if you are interested in this game. Do not watch a play through of it, try the demo, see if your engaged and then buy the game. This review is spoiler free.

A lovely crafted indie detective thriller, with a fantastic narrative story provided me with a very enjoyable and gripping 3/4 hours of game play on my first play through. The game has been painstakingly crafted down to every individual element, and it really shows, but this love creates a gripping, edge of your seat experience which will make you truly engage with every character and feel every emotion in a short space of time. The time setting is fantastic, blending a feel of early 2000 technology, with modern software and interface feel. When the game says use headphones, I usually disagree. But this is one of the rare examples which playing with headphones or a decent speaker set-up takes this from a game to a true experience.

The game has got an excellent blend of mixed media, cinematic and a truly atmospheric score that intertwines with the narrative in a beautiful way to create this experience. Throughout the game it makes you constantly think, am I making the right choices, is this how I solve this puzzle, and gives you everything you need to figure these out in a well executed manner without holding your hand too much. Even the achievements have been carefully thought out to provide you just enough information that your inquisitive brain wants to fully unravel and unlock each one.

Do I wish the game was longer? Yes. Am I disappointing by this? No, I loved every second of my playtime and strongly look forward to what the developer and his talented contributors bring next. Would I consider buying a future DLC expansion? Easily, this has been the most engaged with a game I've been for a very long time, and I would love to see what the developer brings to the operative universe next. 

This game is truly, one of those rare indie gems, that brings the passion and story into an over saturated gaming market, and really makes you wish more development companies (Especially AAA) had the same mentality and craft.

RIDICULOUSLY short and with a wholly unsatisfying storyline ending all round that I'll be sure not to spoil, but that is both predictable, yet entirely short of explanation. Just as you think the game and story is about to really get going...the game ends with little to no answers.

I'm utterly bemused that THIS is the final released version of the game.

I think it's important to go into this game with the proper expectations.

This is not a "choices matter" game when it comes to narration, and the puzzle solving is also pretty minimal when it comes to interactivity. There are a few hidden things you can find but for the most part you're mainly going to be going through the motions and left-clicking your way through the story in around 3 hours.

As it is, I'd say the game is more of an interactive visual novel, and maybe a proof of concept of something that could be done using these bones as a framework for a bigger project where actions and choices have consequences down the line, and where puzzles eventually become less hand-holdy or trivial as you progress through a longer story.

This is still nice as an atmospheric story-driven game with a good ambiance that will keep you entertained for an evening, and hopefully if the game does well enough, we could eventually see a more fully-realized version of what this game appears to want to do, but can't due to its relatively small scope.

I don't know what I just experienced, but it probably will be one of the games that will randomly pop up back into my head every now and then.
The premise of the story is nothing new, you are a new operator at a police force and have to help people remotely, even some story strings are kinda cliche, but that doesn't mean it's badly written. Because I may be damned is the execution well done. While some plottwists are predictable, some are also coming out of nowhere, and are executed very well. Combine this with the developers display of their usage of sound, they just hit that much harder. The visuals of the game are also quite nice and well done, they just fit the atmosphere, especially the sequences between scenes, they really have that very special melancholic feeling for them going, of which I can only name a handful of titles that pull them off.

I really recommend this game as an experience to make, and who knows, maybe I won't be the only one who now has a worm called "The Operator" infiltrating their brain.

A very enjoyable detective thriller that's spent mostly looking at the same computer screen, tastefully emulating a simple, proprietary FBI desktop you'd see in the background of 90s movies. Even so, the gameplay is varied, as you gain access to more and more tools and programs to use in your cases, and the tasks or cases themselves vary a lot. 
One particular case that involves a manual was one of the most memorable gaming experiences I've had recently. It was very tense and had me fully immersed in my current task. You'll know it when you get to it.

Speaking of immersion, you occasionally get breaks from the screen (as you should in real life as well) as your character steps away to end the day and get home, or walk to a nearby destination. These intermissions are very well done and put you in the character's shoes, not to mention let the both of you unwind before the next day of cracking cases.

The mystery is engaging and gives you just enough clues at just the right pace to let you put the puzzle pieces together yourself. Don't take this as a negative, this is the game rewarding you for paying attention, using your notepad and attempting to connect the dots yourself.

For the price of one movie ticket and a box of popcorn you'll get much more than the average flick and support a great developer. I hope to see more in the future.

When I played the demo for The Operator, I knew I was onto something special. I gave it a spin on release day and liked it so much I did a second run-through to pick up all the pieces I missed and see the alternate paths I didn't take the first time.

The Operator's premise is simple; you're an operator for the FDI who handles agent's queries. An agent on the ground will send you photos and videos of what they're seeing, and you have to find the information the agent wants. This includes finding the data or the discrepancy and clicking on it, Papers Please style. And your first day doesn't even finish before something seriously odd starts happening.

The Operator comes in at 3-4 hours of playtime, with an extra hour or two if you decide to replay for all the tidbits like I did. At its price point, some people may dislike that it doesn't hold up to the golden ratio of "one dollar for one hour of game time." Fortunately, this game proves the positive side of the adage "you get what you pay for," because it's by no means an ordinary game.

From the excellent story, to the gripping twists, to the fully voiced characters and the brain-melting puzzles, The Operator is well worth the asking price. My absolute favourite part of the game is its sound design; there are musical stings when evidence appears, and little ramp-ups when a case progresses. My fave parts in the game happened because the game detected that I'm on the right track with solving a puzzle and ramped up the music in response. It gives an incredible cinematic feel that makes you feel like you're in a movie.

I understand that most people will probably feel uneasy paying what the developer asks to get 3-4 hours of gameplay, and if that's you, I recommend wishlisting and coming back when it's on sale. But if you can bite the bullet, you'll find that the game will be more than happy to make every last cent worthwhile.

[b]IF YOU LIKE THIS, TRY:[/b] Home Safety Hotline
This game shares a similar length, premise, and price of another fave of mine; Home Safety Hotline. While The Operator builds on suspense, thrill, and high-stake moments, Home Safety Hotline is surreal, fantastical, and even a little but humorous. As such, if The Operator leaves you wanting more, I recommend this one, too.
